speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
During my absence yesterday the attention of the House was drawn to an accident at Val Brillant station on the Intercolonial railway. This morning 1 received this letter, which gives all the information t have in connection with the matter:
Moncton, N.B., March 23, 1916. Dear Mr. Reid:
I regret to report that at 11.05 p.m., March 21, immediately in front of Val Brillant station, an accident occurred which resulted in the death of fireman Felix Lagouffde, Able St. Am-and, of Ste. Louise, and Jos. Thibault, of Saya-bec, who were riding in a car containing five horses. Engineer William Killam died yesterday as a result of his injuries. Engineer H. Maisey and fireman McNeish are still in a serious condition owing to injuries received.
The accident consisted of a front end collision between two double header freight trains, probably caused by the disregarding of orders on the part of the north bound extra. Investigation being held.
Three engines are badly damaged and the fourth requires to go to the shop for repairs. Six cars of the west bound freight were badly damaged, including one car containing ' five horses and two men above reported.
The main line was blocked twelve hours on account of this accident.
Will advise you further as to monetary loss later when I get further reports.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) F. P. Gutelius.
(Later.)
Coroner's Verdict re Val Brillant given last night is as follows:
" Accident caused by collision between trains at Val Brillant and that no blame is attached to any one except engineer Killam on engine 31.''
This was the engineer of the leading engine on north bound extra who died. Evidence so far points to the fact that he was asleep. Had ample rest before leaving and was on . duty about eleven hours at the time of accident. Our investigation being started Campbellton today.	.
(Sgd.) F. P. Gutelius.
The point raised in the message I read to the House was that the accident was caused by the congestion of cars on the sidings. I am glad to learn that such is not the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We are having an investigation; but from the general manager, who is at present in Ottawa, I understand that both freight trains were supposed to stop at the station and make a crossing; that this train evidently ran through without stopping at all; and that that is probably how the accident occurred.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Minister oi the Interior), the House went into committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that patents of land included in the St. Peters's Indian reserve, in the county of Selkirk, in the province of Manitoba, issued by His Majesty lie confirmed and made good, (a) in cases where lands were unsold and were held by Indian patentees on the first day of June, 1915 ; (b) in cases where the additional sum of one dollar for each acre of such lands included in such patent or sale, together with interest at the rate of five per cent per annum from the first day of June, 1915, until payment has been or is paid to His Majesty ; and (c) in cases where the owner gives His Majesty a lien creating a first charge upon the lands for the sum of one dollar for each acre of such lands included in such patent or sale, payable in five equal instalments with interest at five per centum per annum from the first day of June, 1915; the first of such instalments and interest to be due and payable on the first day of June, 1916 ; and that procedure be prescribed for the effecting and discharge of the said lien; and that in any enactment based upon this resolution it be provided that such enactment shall be deemed to have come into force on the first day of June, 1915.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It will hardly be necessary to enter into an elaborate explanation for the benefit of the older members of the House, as to why this resolution has been introduced, because it has reference to a matter which formed the theme of discussion both inside and outside of this House for several years. It will refresh the memory of some hon. members on the subject when I recall that in September, 1907,, a band of Indians, known as the St. Peters band, occupying a reserve adjacent to the town of Selkirk, surrendered their lands to be disposed of in order to allow the development of the town and of the adjacent neighbourhood. Objections were taken to the .manner of that surrender. It was considered to be null and void, partly by reason of the fact that the interpretation placed upon the law which states that before the surrender could be valid it must have been approved of by a majority of the male members ,of the band. That was interpreted at the time to mean a majority of the male members who attended the meeting at which the vote on the question of the surrender was taken. 'Those who objected to the surrender also contended that the meeting was not called properly; that it was held at the wrong time of the year to give the Indians an opportunity of being
heard; that it was held on too short notice; that improper overtures were made to the Indians at the meeting, in order to induce them to vote in favour of this surrender; that the hall in which the meeting was held was too small to admit the crowd, and that a number of Indians were outside the building and had not an opportunity to hear what was going on within, so that many of them voted in ignorance of the terms of the surrender. As a result of the objections, the registrar in the land titles office in Manitoba refused to register the title. A petition from some of the Indians was presented to the Provincial Government, asking the 'Government to cause an inquiry to be made into the method of the surrender and into whether the surrender was valid or otherwise. The Provincial Government appointed a commission of three county court judges: Judge Prud-homme, Judge Eocke, and Judge Myers. This commission went thoroughly into the circumstances, and, as a result of their investigation two reports were handed in, a majority report signed by Judge Prud-homme and Judge Locke, and a minority report signed by Judge Myers. The majority report was in effect, that the surrender should be declared null and void, and this principally by reason of the fact-although ' other reasons were also given-that it did not conform to the statute requiring a majority of the male members qtf the band to vote in its favour; that Judge Myers reported that the provisions of the Act had, in effect, been complied with. Owing to the report of this commission, the registrar still refused to pass favourably upon the titles, and the matter has since remained in that unsettled condition. It was claimed at the time that the Indians had not received full value for their lands. Of the 45,000 acres, in round numbers, that constituted the reserve, some were allotted to the individual Indians (I think 16 acres per head), amounting in all to some 18,600 acres. The greater portion of these lands were sold individually by the Indians. Other lands included in the 45,000 acres-between 15,000 and 16,000 acres-were sold at public auction at an average price, I believe, of about $5.65 per acre. It was claimed that the Indians had not been fairly dealt with; that, ae usual upon such occasions, advantage had been taken of the Indians by the private purchasers, and that the sale had not been conducted in such manner as to ensure the most competition. At any rate, this Gov-

ernment felt that the Indians had not been fairly dealt with, and that the surrender had not been valid. Consequently, some two years ago or thereabouts, the Indian Department handed this case over to the Justice Department with instructions to take whatever action they in their wisdom should deem necessary. The case was entered in the Exchequer Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Between what parties?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Government on the one hand, and the purchasers of the lands on the other. After a time, overtures were made by the purchasers of these lands desiring to effect settlement with the Government without having the case proceed to trial. Negotiations were conducted for some considerable time between the Justice Department and the barrister representing the purchasers of the lands, and for a long time they failed to arrive at any satisfactory solution of the difficulty. In June of last year, in view of that uncertainty that always exists with regard to the termination of legal cases-for whichever party lost there would be an appeal to the Privy Council-also in view of the fact that the development of the country adjacent to the town of Selkirk would be held up, and that the purchasers of these lands would be placed in an unenviable position, it was deemed advisable to accept an offer which was eventually made by the purchasers of the lands. It was decided that we should confirm the surrender and allow the titles to be passed upon favourably by the registrar, upon the payment of an additional dollar per acre by the purchasers of the land. This would mean, in round numbers, an addition to the Indian Fund of about $43,000 or $45,000. The Registrar of Titles in the province of Manitoba, after some correspondence last summer with the Solicitor General and with the Indian Department, decided that he would pass favourably upon those lands if the Superintendent' Genera] of Indian Affairs would give the assurance that at the next session of Parliament he would introduce an Act to confirm the surrender, and the present titles of the land, upon the payment to the registrar of this additional dollar per acre, and that, in the case of those who are not paying in cash, we should take a first lien on the land. That assurance was given by me as Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, after consultation with my colleagues. Hence this resolution has been introduced, and
fMr Roche!
upon it a Bill will be founded. It is not necessary for me to enter into a minute history of the charges and counter-charges which were made in regard to this matter. In concrete form, the matter stands just as I have explained it.

This question of the sale of St. Peters Indian Reserve has been before the House so frequently that I am sure hon. members will not care to hear it discussed at any great length on this occasion. At the same time, it is in order that it should be pointed out that the action now taken by this Government is a complete and absolute justification of the action of the previous Government and a denial of all the charges, allegations and insinuations that were made against that Government by hon. gentlemen opposite, who were then in opposition, and in particular the hon. membeT for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), who, I observe, is not in his place to-day. I cannot imagine how any other conclusion can be reached from the proposed action of the Government. If the statement made by the minister to-day is read in conjunction with the statements that were formerly made by members on the other side of the House it will be seen that their contentions have been absolutely disproved on investigation by the Government now in power, or else the Government now in power is lending itself in every degree to the alleged injustice that was done the Indians and the alleged mishandling of the public business of which the late Government was said, to be guilty. The horn, member for Selkirk, and other members who took it upon themselves to make the contention, said that the lands dealt with were of a value of $15 an acre and upwards. These lands had been sold at an average price of $5 or $6 an acre, by public auction and by private sale, and the contention was that the Indians had been cheated to the extent of a minimum of at teast $10 an acre, or double the price they received for the land. To-day the minister proposes to wipe the slate cleap upon consideration of the purchasers of this land paying an additional amount, not of $10 an acre, but of $1 an acre. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, either the contentions that were made against the action 'of the late Government have no justification, or else the action of the present Government has no justification, I certainly cannot congratulate the Government, when it is compelled to negative the contentions

of its supporters, that it has not done so gracefully, and, I will take the liberty of saying, honestly, by admitting that the transaction was in all respects what they now in effect admit it to have been. There never was any ground whatever for the contentions that were made by members of the then opposition in regard to this land transaction.
I shall take the liberty of saying that the fact that the purchasers of this land were not able to>
register their title, under the administration of the late Manitoba Government, was neither more nor less than a political hold-up, arranged between private members on the then Opposition side of the House and the then Manitoba Government, which had control of that registration, a political hold-up in the expectation that some political or personal profit could be made to accrue to the parties concerned. If the registrar of land titles of the province of Manitoba was at that time justified in refusing registration of these titles because the surrenders had not been legally made, he certainly was not warranted in accepting registration of them now, when there is no further evidence that the surrender was legally made. The surrender stands just as it did before. If this officer refused registration because he considered a sufficient price was not paid for the land, then I submit that the payment of an additional dollar an acre does not warrant him in accepting registration. The purchasers of these lands were entitled 'to the property they had bought for the money they had agreed to pay, and it was up to this Government, or to those who were contending against the validity of 'the former transaction, to prove that that transaction was not straight and in all respects according to the larw. They could not ,do it, although they have had nine years in which to do it, and the result is that they have given up the attempt and have practically surrendered to the position as it was before. I perhaps speak somewhat strongly in regard to this matter. Having been the minister in charge of Indian Affairs at the time the surrender was taken, I was subjected to a very great deal of very venomous and unwarranted criticism, both by those who knew better and by those who knew nothing at all about the case. Therefore I feel warranted in taking this opportunity of placing before the House, and thereby before the country, the facts as to the complete exoneration of the officers of the department
and of myself, and of the purchasers of the land, in fact all who were connected with the transaction, on the authority of the Minister of the Interior and on the responsibility of the Government of which he is a member, as shown by the action that he is now taking. Not to delay the committee, I simply wish to say that the surrender of the St. Peters reserve was in the interest of the Indians; it was in the interest of the surrounding community; it was in the interest of the province and in the interest of the country generally. It received the approval of all those several interests, and the fact that it was delayed in its execution until the present time was simply, I repeat, a political holdup, the result of which will be, I fancy, the retirement of one or two members of this House to private life when the next election takes place.
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Solicitor General:) The hon. gentleman's arraignment of the resolution proceeds on the assumption that it is a justification of the action of the late Government in regard to the St. Peters reserve. He did not favour the House with any explanation, or present to us any foundation for his contention. He forgets that the worst crimes are those which do not admit of expiation, and the worst forms of political malpractice are those which cannot be visited with an adequate remedy. This is one of those forms. The late Government took upon itself to adopt certain methods, and also later on to ratify the methods adopted by those acting under them, with regard to this legislation, which, at the time, justly brought upon the Government very severe criticism in the country. The late Government remained in power, however, for some time after the reserve was given up, and after the whole transaction was, so far as it was concerned, closed. In the meantime many other considerations reared their heads and complicated the whole subject with dif-Acuities that prevented an appropriate remedy being bad.
Now, what are those considerations? It is clear to every one who has had any experience, either in business or in litigation, that the tying up of the title to land that is involved in protracted litigation brings with it very severe injury and a very severe penalty upon thosB who are in no way connected, and indeed are in no way primarily concerned, with the cause of the litigation. That is ' true even in regard to special

parcels of land that have in the past been involved in long litigious proceedings. Here we have a very pronounced case of that kind; here we have a case of the continuance of litigation which necessarily could not be set in motion until some years after the transaction itself transpired, and some years after various innocent interests necessarily had arisen; here we have a case of not one special parcel, but of literally thousands of acres of land in which the whole community is interested, that must necessarily he tied up as' to its title, and in respect of which development must stop, until that litigation proceeds to its termination. It must be clear to the hon. member for Edmonton that, no matter how ill-founded and no matter how inherently wrong the original transaction was; no matter how unjust it was to the Indians and to those connected with them, there necessarily will come the interests of 'the community which must suffer by the only remedy that can be adopted to set right the wrong that was done. Consequently that must he taken into consideration by a Government that proceeds to: set right the wrong; that must be taken into consideration when- any offer of settlement presents itself that enables us to" do at least some form of justice, without involving too much injustice with it, to those who were not guilty of the original transaction. In that connection it must he borne in mind that the town of Selkirk itself, which is situated beside a large portion of these lands, is concerned in removing the cloud that rests upon the title. It appears that some industrial enterprises had located in the neighbourhood of, and I believe right on, some of the lands concerned, and consequently the town of Selkirk, which, as a corporation, which as an industrial enterprise, had nothing whatever to do with the original wrong, had nothing whatever to do with the original surrender, was in no way in complicity with the late Government in what they d^d, suffered and had no remedy that could be applied, entirely irrespective of the wrong that gave rise to the necessity of a remedy.
Furthermore, the owners of the lands adjoining the town of Selkirk, outside of what may be termed municipal interests, are concerned to see that somebody gets to own these lands, to know who does own them, and to see that the lands will admit of that development which adds to the value of adjoining lands. These owners are innocent parties in every sense, and we 
should take care to visit on them as little as possible the inevitable penalty that comes from tying up the title of these lands.
There is another consideration still. While the surrender may have been invalid, while in my humble judgment it was invalid legally, and while I think that that would have been the ultimate decision of the courts, this is this fact, that there were some concerned with that sale who were by no means as guilty as others, and there ' were some whose interest subsequently arose, and in whom there could be no guilt at all. The men who did wrong, at all events the men who were enabled to do wrong by the action of the late Government, who perpetrated the wrong upon the Indians, were able to get away with the results of their wrongdoing before this Government came into power. They imposed upon the Indian, they took advantage of the opportunity, and as soon as they had done feo, they made a sale claiming that they had a right to do so, and relying on the Government to say that it was a just and honourable action; and the innocent purchaser comes in and finds that these men have got away with the money and that there is no way of recovering it. Many who are now interested in these lands are not those who themselves took advantage of the opportunity afforded them by the late Administration, and consequently it would be unfair to exact from them that portion of their profit, or whatever you may call it, that actually has already been disposed of by the really guilty ones who went before them.
All these considerations must be kept in mind, and in the presence of them it is impossible to do actual justice. It may be impossible to do what one would describe as substantial justice. All we can do in the presence of these facts and circumstances is to meet the case in the most adequate way we can; and it was deemed best, indeed, the only way that a settlement could be arrived at, to accept a certain amount per acre in respect of those who held the lands obtained at that sale, or who obtained from the Indians lands by virtue of the surrender. Consequently, any one who eo holds these lands must, before their title can be made complete, pay to the Government of Canada one dollar per acre in respect of them. The Indian himself of course does not have that .to pay. Those Indians who hold what they got there hold it still, and hold it without any cloud, or without any lien on the part of the Government of Canada.

The hon. gentleman says that the action of the registrar of Manitoba was a political hold-up, executed by the Registrar General at the instance of the then Government of Manitoba, and I presume of the present Government of Canada. I do not know what he means by a political hold-up.
I did not say it was by the present Government; the hold-up was by the Provincial Government of Manitoba, before this Government came into power-.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend says that the Manitoba Government used the judiciary of the province as an instrument to carry out a hold-up. That is the charge?
That is the charge.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend says
that is the charge.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I did not say that they used the judiciary. They exercised their authority over their appointed officials,

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I said the judiciary and the hon. gentleman assented. It must have been the judiciary that they used as their instrument, because the judiciary of Manitoba, by a majority of two to one, decided that the reserve was not legally taken, and that it was the duty of the Registrar to refuse to pass the title.
The point is, who was the registrar, and who appointed him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The point is, who were the judiciary. The judiciary came to that decision, and my hon. friend must take either one horn of the dilemma or the other; he must either say that we were right in our contention, or that in this political hold-up the judiciary of the province was utilized as an instrument.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I know of no other
course he can take.

The judiciary did not
make the hold-up; it was the officers of the Government of Manitoba.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The judiciary found
that the contention of the then Opposition was correct,, that the reserve was improperly taken, and that justice bad not been done to the Indian, and consequently, as a result of the finding of the judiciary, the registrar of the province refused to pass the title.
He refused it first.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know that he did; I do not think he did. But, if he did refuse it first, his action was determined to be right and proper by the judiciary. But I think my hon. friend is wrong; I do not think he refused it until after the finding of the judges.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: And on the recommendation of Chief Justice Howell.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, and on the recommendation of Chief Justice Howell. I need make no remark on the eminence of that member of the judiciary of Manitoba. So much for the charge that there was a political hold-up. After all is said and done in so far as this settlement is effected, the principle for which we have all along contended is vindicated. The Indian who has lost is the Indian who now benefits. His fund benefits to the extent of about $40,000. No one contends that $40,000 represents the amount which my hon. friends opposite permitted the men to get away with, but the $40,000 represents the amount As nearly as we can judge which we are able to get, and which will do a measure of substantial justice in the presence of the circumstances that have arisen, and which deny to us the possibility cf securing actual justice for those who suffered by reason of the action of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Perhaps I may explain before I sit down that the Bill doe? not force a settlement upon any one. Any one who feels that he has no right to pay this money may continue the litigation. I do not know that any will avail themselves of that opportunity, because, speaking frankly, the the amount is not high; but at all events it must not be understood that we are forcing this by way of a levy. We are simply saying to those who are ready to pay that the offer should be accepted, and to that extent that the land should be freed from the cloud and removed from the terrors of litigation.
Have the Indians been consulted in regard to this proposed settlement?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
mean the 'Indians themselves?
Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Government of
Canada represents the Indians; the Indians are our wards, and we are making the settlement as their guardians.
That does not answer my question. I would like to know whether or not the Indians themselves have been consulted with regard to this proposed settlement.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have had many representations from the Indians approving of the settlement.

My hon. friend knows perfectly well that, in regard to disposal of their lands, there is a mode of consulting the Indians. Notice is given of the meeting at which the Indians are allowed to assemble and the matter is brought before them, and they determine as to the action they should take. What occurs to me is that, according to the view which has been presented by the Solicitor General, and also, I think, by the Minister of the Interior, the surrender was void. If it was void, then the lands still belong to the Indians. One or the other must be true; either the surrender was good and valid, and the Indians parted with their property in a perfectly legal way, or the surrender was void, and, therefore, the lands still belong to the Indians. Now, I do not think that the Government really relies upon the contention that the surrender was void, for they propose to make a .settlement which would effectually take from the Indians any possible claim they would have to these lands. The Indians ought to have been called together and consulted in the regular way as to the' disposition which would be made of the interests which the Government contends they still had in the lands, notwithstanding the surrender which was alleged to have taken place. I understand the Objection to the alleged surrender on the part of this Government, and upon the part of the registrar in Manitoba, who was an appointee of the Roblin Government, was that the Indians were not properly notified, that they were not properly called together in council, ant^ did not, therefore, have a fair opportunity of considering the proposed surrender. But now the Government, notwithstanding that it is pretending to this House that there is no surrender; that the proceedings were wholly void, and that the Indians still remain the owners of the lan^s, is proposing, without consulting the Indians at all, and without calling them together in council, to ask this Parliament to completely and absolutely alienate their rights, whatever they may be. That is the position in which this Government stands. It does seem to

me that the Government is not in a position to say that the 'surrender which took place some years ago was void, because from its conduct it must be inferred that it is of the opinion that in law and in equity the Indians have no title to these lands, that they have surrendered their title. But, as there is an opportunity to obtain from those people who had bought the land and paid their money, an additional amount which they are willing to pay rather than be compelled to go to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and to incur large expenses of litigation, the Government is making that an excuse for settlement, and is now coming to Parliament and asking it to ratify the proposed settlement simply because it is getting an additional sum of $.1 per acre out of the purchasers of this land. More than that, the excuse that is made by the Solicitor General is that there are some people who are absolutely innocent, and there are some people who have been guilty of very grave wrong-doing. Yet, the Government is proposing to treat all alike on the principle that the sun shines equally on the innocent and the guilty. Does the sun of this Government shine equally, and with the same intensity, upon those who are guilty as upon those who are absolutely innocent of any wrong-doing? The result is that the innocent man, the man who has been guilty of no wrong-doing whatever, who acted in the most perfect good faith, who paid his money believing the transfer was altogether just, proper, and legal, in order to get his title, is compelled to pay the same amount of money that this Government is exacting from the man who, it believes, was guilty of very grave wrongdoing. Is that fair? Is there any principle of justice in that?
The Solicitor General puts forward another excuse. He says that they might appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and that the title of the land might be held to be void, but that it would take a long period of time to decide. This Government has been in power now for upwards of four years and an ordinary appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council takes, at the very outside, twelve months. Appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are disposed of rather speedily, and if the Government had chosen to bring this matter to the test of law within a reasonable time after it came into office, this Whole question would have been settled long ago. But after wait-

ing for four years, the Government comes now, and, for a paltry additional sum of $1 per acre-which it is not exacting in cash but which it is allowing the
4 p.m. grantees to extend over a period of years, and upon which they are paying 5 per cent interest-it is proposing to make this settlement by which those who are innocent of wrongdoing and those who are guilty are put in a position of absolute equality. If there was fraud, if there was wrongdoing, if the surrender was absolutely void, then the Indians own the land. If the land was worth $15 per acre, as was alleged some years ago so strongly by hon. gentlemen who are now occupying the treasury benches, this Government ought not to have compromised for the small sum of $1 per acre, but the Government ought to have carried the case to the highest court in the realm and had it settled long, long since.
There is one other consideration to which my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has referred. The official of the Roblin Government in Manitoba declined to recognize the transfer because the surrender was void and therefore the transfers were void. I would like to know how it comes that he afterwards recognized these transfers at the instance of this Government. If they were ever void they are void to-day. This Government, without legislation, has no power to make them valid, and how is it that at the instance of this Government the registrar of Manitoba has allowed to be recorded certain transfers which previously he had held to be absolutely void and which he had held he had no power to place on record? The Government is to-day seeking retroactive legislation to make legal what they say the registrar of Manitoba has done, and in order to validate what the Minister of the Interior did a good many months ago, and which he did, according to the Government's view, absolutely without legal authority.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is forgetting that action of this official in Manitoba of which he complains was committed by him as an official of the new Norris Government some months after that Government came in.
By the new Norris Government? At whose instance? Was it the same official?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly, but under
the instructions of the new Attorney General.

If it was under the instructions of the new Attorney General, then that means that the new Attorney General of Manitoba believes that the surrender was absolutely valid and perfectly legal. That must be the opinion of the new Attorney General of Manitoba, and it is a proper opinion.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
You do not get the
reason there.

But notwithstanding
that the opinion of the Attorney General of Manitoba is that the transfer was perfectly legal and valid, and that the people who paid their money have a right to have their deeds of transfer registered, this Government has threatened to carry the case to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council unless these people, innocent and guilty alike, pay into the treasury the sum, according to the Solicitor General, of $1 per acre, extending that over an unlimited period of time and paying interest at 5 per cent per annum. It does seem to me that the action of this Government in this respect is not defensible. Either that transfer was legal or it was illegal. If it was illegal, then the Indians are entitled to their lands; they are entitled to be consulted; they are entitled to be called together in the regular way to be informed of their legal position, and their rights should be guarded by this Government, which is the trustee for the Indians. I would like to know what right a trustee in an ordinary case would have to act as the Minister of the Interior is acting in this case in reference to these Indians whose trustee the Minister of the Interior is. Hon. gentlemen upon the other side of the House have alleged th|at this land was worth the very large sum of $15 per acre. They have alleged that fraud was perpetrated; that the interests of'the Indians were sacrificed, and that an average of ten dollars per acre was unlawfully taken from them. Yet, to-day, without consulting the Indians, the Government ask to have what they have done confirmed simply by providing an additional fund for the Indians of the sum of only one dollar per acre as compared with ten dollars per acre which they alleged the Indians were unlawfully deprived of in the past.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the reasoning of the hon. member for St. John (Mr Pugsley) would lead to the conclusion that no lawsuit ever should be settled. He argues, on the one



hand, that a settlement should meet all the requirements of what would happen if the Government should succeed in ite litigation, and he finds fault if we do not get that. Then, on the other hand, he finds fault with this settlement because the parties settling and making the payment are not going to get all that they would get if it was decided that they were right; that is to eay, that they were to retain the land and pay nothing. I have always understood that it was in the nature of a settlement and compromise that the parties should get together, basing their action necessarily on the leaving aside for the moment of the absolute determination of who is right and who is wrong; and, that this Government should be willing under those circumstances to come to a settlement which does not produce all the results that a successful lawsuit would produce, seems to me only the ordinary conduct of any one who joins in a settlement. We did entertain-and I may say that we entertain still-a very strong conviction that that surrender was illegal, and was ineffective; but our predecessors in office had so arranged matters that, out of that surrender, it must necessarily follow, if our view was right, that the Indian would suffer eerious loss. I am not in a position to speak of the exact amount of that loss, but we are quite satisfied that the bringing about of that surrender in the way in which it was brought about, necessarily created a situation where, if it stood, the Indian was going to suffer considerable loss. The action of our predecessors not only entailed that loss if the surrender stood valid, but, furthermore, it created a condition where, inevitably, what happened was to be expected, that is to say, that persons not connected with the original transaction, and having before them the fact that the then representatives of the Indians had sanctioned and approved what had been done and were standing behind the titles, invested their money in those properties, which, as the hon. Solicitor General has pointed out, were passed over, enabling those who were parties to the original transaction, which we believe and still believe to have been tainted with fraud, to pocket their profits. Creating that situation, our predecessors created a situation where just what has happened necessarily must have been anticipated, where, if the surrender were set aside, as we contend it ought to be, then necessarily there must be suffering entailed upon per-
sons who, to the extent of having acted in good faith, were innocent in respect of the validity of their title. I do not go so far as to say that, as a matter of law or even as a matter of justice, a man who acquires a property to which the vendor has no title, is necessarily entitled to claim that he is wrongfully treated, when the invalidity of his title is determined, because it is no doubt his duty to inquire into the validity of the title. But necessarily the action of our predecessors, as we understand it, not only gravely prejudiced the Indian, but created a condition of affairs where this grave prejudice to innocent third persons was possible, and also created a condition where it was only reasonably to be anticipated that that injury to third persons would come about. Now, we are in face of a case of that kind where, if our view is right, the Indian was deprived of his property. We are, of course, in face of people who seriously contend that oqr position is invalid. That does not alter our view about our position, but we are not so unreasonable as to treat our opinion as infallible -and I think the hon. gentleman himself will admit that it is not the very best lawyer who, because of the strength of his own opinion, will always repudiate a proposed settlement which gives some advantage to his client, even though it does not give his client all that he is entitled to. Settlements practically invariably are of that" nature. There is no doubt room for difference of opinion-and in saying that I do not depart at all from the opinion which I have already expressed, and which I entertain very strongly-and there is always uncertainty in the determination of questions of law, and more particularly I may say, do you find yourself exposed to uncertainty when you present yourself before a court with a question of law, the abstract determination of which, in either one respect or the other, must necessarily entail hardship to innocent people on one side or the other. I think any lawyer, dealing with a case of that kind and looking at the question of the probable result of his case, would feel that be was bound to give serious consideration to the possible effects on the determination of the question of that condition of affairs, namely, one where a determination in absolute accord with the strict law must necessarily entail hardship upon innocent third persons. Those are the conditions in which that case stands. Furthermore, with regard to the Indian, this, I think, is fairly to 'be pointed

out that, assuming the absolute success of the Government as the representative of the Indian, assuming a judgment in the sense which we contend, and still believe the judgment ought to be rendered, there would remain the fact that such persons as dealt with this property innocently and in good faith would be, as a matter of simple equity, entitled to represent to the Government of Canada that the Government of Canada at the time, then acting as the agent of the Indian, then being the person in whose hands the Indians' interests all were, had failed in its trust to the Indian as we understand it, but being always the trustee of the Indian, who, the outside party has a right to assume, was acting lawfully on his behalf, had brought about and created this situation, causing the serious loss that was entailed upon such parties as were innocent by the judgment that I assume to have been rendered. In that condition of affairs I think it would present a very serious question whether or not a Government, even in the face of a determination of the illegality of all this transaction, would feel called upon to do something to meet the position created by .a Government of Canada and resulting in the suffering of those innocent acquirers. Under all these conditions, it would seem to me, if ever there was a case that was an ideal case to settle, that this was the case, and that, without derogating in the slightest from the earnestness of my conviction that upon the law of the case the Government ought to succeed. The reproach is now made that, in proceeding to make this settlement, we do not make certain that a sufficient surrender has been made. That is equivalent to saying that we do not settle on the basis of having already a judgment determining the question. How are we going to settle with people if we throw their rights back on a determination of the main question? If we settle we must proceed to that settlement without determining absolutely who was right and who was wrong. We realize that the Indian is not getting all that he would get if we succeeded, as I think, from all I have seen of the evidence, that we should. On the other hand, the parties who obtained the property will pay very much less than they would pay if we succeeded. They are getting a clear title, and they are, at all events, paying something to compensate the Indian for the loss entailed upon him. It is said that we ought to discriminate, first finding out who were the innocent and who were the guilty 1301
parties, and not deal with both indiscriminately. That is'one of the questions that would be determined if the lawsuit went on. But we are making a settlement. It is not impossible that some party or parties have had knowledge of this matter that would entail at least a moral responsibility; it may be possible that some of those whom we thought to be in good faith may not have been in good faith, and, on the other hand, that some whom we thought to have been in bad faith may not have been in bad faith. These are questions that would have to be submitted to the court and passed upon. We are getting a settlement because we believe that, on the one side, the Indian is, at all events, securing a measure of compensation, and that, on the other side, we are acting in the public interest, because, as the Solicitor General pointed out, we are acting in such a manner as to enable us to avoid unnecessary loss to such oi these persons as were in good faith. I think that, so far as absence of complaints on their part can show, they stand perfectly willing to make this settlement. Nobody is opposing it. But no man who is in good faith and who believes he has a good	title is
to be forced to make this payment. If he believes that his case is good, he can go on and fight it out. All we propose to do is to make a settlement with those who are willing to make a settlement. There is no doubt the Indian is left without an adequate remedy if we are right; but that is the case with every party who settles his case. In view of the difficulties I have pointed out of doing absolute justice to everybody, even if we succeeded, it seems to me that the criticisms made of this suggested settlement can hardly be justified.

I believe it is an understood principle of British law that every man is held to be innocent until he is proven guilty. We have heard speeches by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) to-day based on the assumption that somebody unnamed is guilty, notwithstanding the fact that although these hon. gentlemen have the authority to go to the proof, they have not gone to the proof. I think it would have been more in accordance with justice, if not in' accord with law as administered by our friends opposite, if these hon. gentlemen had recognized the fundamental principle to which I have referred, and had not repeated, the assertion that wrong had

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have no desire to add to the heat of the hon. member for Edmonton; I do not think that he misapprehended the course I took in the few remarks that I made a little while ago. The hon. gentleman argued that the course that we are taking now is an exoneration of the late Government. I sought to meet that argument, and to contend that our action was no exoneration of the late Government. I did not go back of that and enter into the merits of the original dispute to show where right and wrong was. That was debated in this House for hours, indeed, for days and weeks, and ha? been session after session. I do not think it, is the desire of hon. gentlemen that we should go back into that field of controversy now. I do think that I met the contention of the hon. gentleman by showing that in introducing this legislation we are by no means exonerating the late Administration and are by no means taking a, position inconsistent with the position we took when the late Government wTas in power. That was all I argued. If it is the desire of the hon. gentleman to do so, he can have an opportunity any time he wishes of introducing a motion or otherwise, and we will go back with him over that old ground again; I am just as ready to do it as he is. I think, however, that we have better use for our time on ,the present occasion and better use for our time this session than to do that. I wish to refer, however, to one or two points raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. It is said by the hon. member for St. John-in this he is supported by the hon. member for Edmonton-that we should in this case have gone to the Indian and had him justify our proceeding by accepting this settlement, along the line and parallel to the procedure laid down in the Act for us in respect of a surrender itself.
My contention is not that the Government should do as it is doing. My contention is that the Government should drop the whole affair and allow the property to be registered.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have passed that point; I am dealing with a specific argument of the hon. member for St. John, which was- supported by the. hon. member for Edmonton. He says that the original Act provides- that before a surrender shall be valid the Indians shall be gathered together, and, after certain form of procedure, they shall ratify it by a majority. He says that inasmuch as that is laid down as the procedure before a surrender in the first place shall be valid, we now, proceeding to validate the surrender, should take their consent also to that validation. It is to my mind clear that it is proper that the Indian should be appealed to before so simple a thing as a surrender is taken from him. The band may be quite competent to decide whether or not it is in their interests to abandon their property and accept some other property at a distance away in lieu thereof, and to accept very simple and, very easily understandable terms. That is one thing, but it is quite another thing to argue that we should have gone to the Indians of St. Peters reserve and submitted to them the legal arguments on one side as to the validity of the surrender and the legal arguments- on the other side as to its invalidity, and then ask them to weigh one against the other and decide whether the difference is worth $40,000. That appears to me to be a most absurd proposal to submit to a band of Indians. If they could decide that we had better liberate and emancipate them, act no longer as their guardians, make them ordinary citizens.

I was basing my argument entirely upon the theory advanced by the Government, who are the trustees for the Indians, that there never was a surrender and that the land still remains the land of the Indians. What occurred to me was that, in order to be consistent, the Government ought to have called the Indians together and said: there is an alleged surrender of this land, but in our opinion there has been no surrender. We can settle the matter upon certain such and such terms; we advise you to consent to settlement; we want your approval.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite agree with that if we won, it would be in our interest to do that. Even if we were positively certain that we should succeed, then we would require to go back to the Indian-it would be common sense to do so-and have a surrender taken in the usual way. Then the Indian would have to decide upon issues that the country's laws say he is capable

*of deciding upon. But under the present [DOT]circumstances, to lay before him a legal pro- [DOT] position, to throw controversy into the Indian's camp and ask him to decide the [DOT]question, appears to me to be too absurd for argument. Furthermore, there is the practical fact that the Indians to-day are for the most part away up somewhere north of the lakes, on another reserve. They are scattered more or less to the ends of the earth, making such procedure a practical impossibility. It is said that I have stated that some of those now interested in these lands are innocent parties. They are innocent, in that they are in no way concerned or implicated in the original wrong as we contend it to have been. Yet in another sense they are not; they have taken title from those who were implicated; they derive their title from them, and in a sense, they purchased at their peril. Consequently, it is nothing in the nature of a hold-up to say to those who have bought, knowing the facts, before you are removed from this cloud under which you never should have come, you must pay this compensation to those who were the original owners of the land.

Is the argument of the Solicitor General, in which we are assumed to take an intelligent interest, based upon the justifiability, if I may use such a word, of the contract? Is it that, since the Indians are not able to administer their own affairs and the Government is therefore the guardian of these Indians, we must fall back upon the first principle, and that is the morality of the agreement itself? Is that correct?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid I do not
understand the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Did I understand that Chief Justice Howell had expressed an opinion on this transaction?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In what circumstances?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Chief Justice Howell was appointed, I think, by the previous Government, to examine into certain grievances of these Indians. He did so. When the Commission appointed by the Provincial Government were taking evidence, they summoned him to give evidence and he was asked:
Q. After the surrender you had nothing further to do with the whole matter?-A. No. I made my report and closed it, and the Indians

came swarming up to me here and I took it upon myself to go over to Mr. Macara's office (Mr. Macara being the registrar of land titles) and try to stop the patents going through, for which, in Parliament, I think, I got a lot of abuse.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This puts not altogether a new face upon the case, but simply adds to the opinion I formed from the discussion which went on. I agree altogether with the Minister of Justice, that it is always preferable to settle cases rather than to go to the extremities of the law. But there are eases upon which there can be no settlement. No man will settle a case in which his honour is impugned. He will never accept anything short of a full apology. No trustee has a right to settle a case for his ward upon a question of fraud. He should not do so, he has not the right to do so. This case has long been familiar to the older members of the House, as was stated in the opening remarks of the Minister of the Interior. We have had it up in the House again and again. The contention which was made by gentlemen who now sit upon the Treasury benches and their followers was that the Indians had been cheated; that they had been victims of a fraud; that their lands had been wrongfully sold by the Government of that day; that these lands were worth at least $10 to $15 an acre; that they were sold for something like $5 an acre, and that the Indians were cheated of the balance, amounting to something like $450,000. If the gentlemen who made that contention were sincere and honest when they said the Indians were cheated, they have no cause and no right to do what they are now doing, that is, condone a fraud. This is not an ordinary case of the interpretation of a contract. It is not a question of law. It is a question of fact-were these Indians cheated or not cheated?
Hear, hear, that is what I asked.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If these Indians were cheated, as was asserted by the gentlemen who now sit on the other side of the House, to-day these hon. members are doing nothing else than condoning a fraud, and cheating the Indians of something like $[DOT]400,000. Well, Sir, I do not believe they are doing that. I do not believe that the Indians were cheated. I think the accusations made were wrong, and that this legislation is the best vindication of my friend the then Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), who was responsible for the transaction. Can it be conceived that the hon.

member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), or the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), or the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche), if they really believed what they asserted four, five or six years ago, when in Opposition, that the Indians had been cheated, would to-day consent to the bringing in of such a Bill as this? To me this is a very happy solution of a long standing difficulty, and, I think, a full vindication of the Government that was in office when the transaction took place.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. ROCHE thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 67, relating to the St. Peters Indian Reserve.
I do not wish to be technical, but would it not be necessary to preface this resolution with the statement that it has received the consent and approval of His Royal Highness the Governor General?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I was advised that it was not necessary to do so in this case.
My view would be that, as it deals with the disposal of public lands, it should first receive the approval of His Royal Highness.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: I shall give my decision on this point when the Bill is up for a second reading.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), the House went into committee, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair, to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Judges Act, chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide:
That the salaries of the judges of the Court of Appeal, and of His Majesty's Court of King's Bench, for Saskatchewan, shall be as follows: (a) the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, if he is also the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal, and if not, to the Chief Justice of Appeal, $8,000 per annum; (b) three puisne judges of the Court of Appeal, each $7,000 per annum; (c) the Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench, $7,000 per annum ; (d) five puisne judges of the Court of King's Bench, each $6,000 per annum.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What change is there from the existing law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This resolution is introduced for the purpose of basing upon it an Act to meet a new situation created in the province of Saskatchewan.
By legislation enacted in 1915, that province substituted for its Supreme Court two distinct courts, a court of appeal and a court of first instance, to be called the Court of King's Bench, and determined the number of judges of those prospective courts. The purpose of this legislation is to provide the necessary salaries* for the payment of the judges of the courts so constituted. I may say that we have had very strong representations from the Government of the province as to the necessity of this change in the constitution of the courts, and of our meeting it by providing for the appointment and payment of the judges of those courts. These representations have been confirmed from other sources, by those in a position to know the necessities within the province.

Possibly I should have made these observations when the Speaker was in the chair:	that the
judges of the province of Alberta think they are not too* fairly treated. We have no court of appeal in Alberta, but our judges constitute an appellate division, and so obviate the necessity of creating a court of appeal. Many of our judges who would not otherwise obtain the experience that is obtained by an appeal judge get it in that way. They go out and take trials, and then when they come back they may be allotted to the appellate division for three months, or for six months. They get a taste of appeal work for a portion of the year, and take nisi prius work for the rest of the year.
How many judges have you?

while to the east of us the Chief Justice of (Saskatchewan will draw $1,000 more than the Chief Justice of Alberta. When one considers that the judges of Alberta are discharging the duties of nisi prius judges and appeal court judges I think the case on their behalf is much stronger than it would otherwise be. I would suggest, as I have suggested to the minister, that where an appellate division has been created from the existing judges, without the creation of a court of appeal, these judges who constitute the appellate division should receive the extra remuneration, that would come to them if they were a court of appeal; and also that the Chief Justice should 'at least be placed in the same position as a chief justice of a province in which there is a court of appeal. I realize the difficulties which the Minister of Justice has very frankly stated he would experience in dealing with the question in that way, because it might necessitate dealing with the whole question of judges' salaries, and this is not the time to do that. But if all the judges west of the lakes were to be treated on the .same basis as to salaries as those in Eastern Canada it would involve a charge upon the revenue of but $22,000 per annum in addition to the extra amount that might be paid to the chief Justice of Alberta. I bring this to the attention of the minister because I think he is sympathetic. I feel that dt would be hardly fair to the province in which I live if I did not do so, where judges are discharging the duties of a court of appeal, as in Alberta the Chief Justice, at least, should be in the same position, and have the same status and salary as the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan or of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I appreciate the force
of what has been said by the hon. member for Calgary (Mir. Bennett), always assuming that justice between judges of the different courts and different provinces absolutely necessitates equality. Therefore, I am not disposed to quarrel with the suggestion that the judges in the province of Alberta might possibly be better paid. But the suggestion would come with equal force from the judges in other provinces. To take up the question of the salaries of judges in provinces where their positions are being in no way changed, would necessarily, as a matter of fairness, necessitate our dealing with the whole question of the salaries of judges throughout the country.

I think the reasons are obvious why we should not select this particular moment to deal with these salaries from the -point of vietv of increasing them. I may point out that the position of the judges of Alberta will not be one particle worse because it so happens that, being called upon to provide salaries for the judges of newly established courts, we make these salaries conform to those allotted to the judges of similar courts in other provinces which have similar courts. This does no injury to the judges in Alberta; it leaves them absolutely in statu quo.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No injury, but the subject of envy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. It seems that if you do something for somebody else it is more resented than if you fail to do something for the person complaining. However that may be, I do not want to be understood as speaking otherwise than sympathetically with regard to the position in which the judges of Alberta find themselves, but for the reason I have given I cannot see Why I should pick them out for special treatment now, without justifying similar representations on the part of other provinces, situated as Alberta now is, and raising the whole questtion of judges' salaries.

I do not desire to join issue with my hon. friend, but that is hardly the fact, because there are nine judges in the province of Alberta, and four of them are doing appeal court work all the time. The court is practically sitting all the time, and the other members of the court are doing duty as nisi prius judges. If the province of Alberta constituted and created a court of appeal consisting of a Chief Justice and three puisne judges of the court of appeal, we would be called upon to pay exactly the. same sum as is now being paid in Saskatchewan. It would not increase the number of judges but would give each of those four judges $1,000 a year more. It does seem anomalous that those gentlemen are performing the duties of court of appeal judges, the same as in Saskatchewan-only we call it an appellate division-and that they are not getting the same emolument.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not dispute the
anomaly at all, but there are other anomalies. I would not be dealing with the judges of Saskatchewan to-day if it were not for the absolute necessity that is created by this legislation. The legislation of the

* province of Saskatchewan when brought into force, as it is intended to be, by a proclamation of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, will create a situation where there will be no courts in Saskatchewan unless we provide judges and salaries for the newly constituted courts, because they have abolished the existing courts. That is the reason I am dealing with Saskatchewan. With reference to judges in other provinces who may think that their salaries are too low, I am acting more in their interest by dealing with the judges of Saskatchewan in the direction of levelling them up with those who are better off rather than levelling them down to the level of those who are not so well off. This legislation may, when it is enacted, afford an additional argument to strengthen the position of those judges who have the lower salaries. I do not think it is possible for me to single out the judges of Alberta for exceptional treatment or to take up the whole question of salaries of judges at the present time. It is necessary that we should deal with the salaries of the judges of these new courts in Saskatchewan and the only way in which we could get equality with the judges of Alberta by means of this Bill would be by reducing the salaries that it is proposed to give to these judges of the newly constituted court in Saskatchewan. I do not understand that anybody suggests that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Everybody
knows that the Minister of Justice has no alternative in this matter, and that he is compelled to bring in this legislation. This is in consequence of the extraordinary provision of our constitution which places the constitution of courts in the provinces, and the payment of judges in the Dominion Parliament. So long as the constitution remains as it is there will always be anomalies, such as there have been since Confederation, and which have made the position of the Minister of Justice not a bed of roses. I am satisfied that my hon. friend has been pestered day after day and year after year with applications for the rectifying of inequalities in the salaries of judges not only in Alberta but in every other province in the Dominion. There are inequalities that cannot be justified- as between the remuneration of judges performing similar duties in different parts of the Dominion. How this condition of affairs is to be remedied it is difficult to see except by an amendment of the constitution which nobody would be prepared to advocate at the present time, and I am afraid that the judges of Alberta will have to remain under what they think is an injustice. As long as they see the judges in a neighbouring province receiving better pay than they are, they will always say that they are not being properly treated. I was a good many years in office and I am familiar with this question.

We will pass an
Act in the Alberta Legislature next year creating a Court of Appeal and then our judges get the added salary.

The population in our province is equal to that of Saskatchewan, the service is performed, and performed very satisfactorily indeed, by six judges and the chief justice at salaries of $7,000 for the chief justice, -and $6,000 for each judge. It is now proposed, because the Legislature of Saskatchewan chooses to create an Appellate Court, to provide for ten judges altogether, including two chief justices at higher salaries than are paid in Alberta. It is proposed that these chief justices should get $8,000 each, the judges of appeal $7,000, the chief justice of the court of King's Bench $7,000 and the puisne judges $7,000 each. If this were not a year where economy was absolutely essential, the minister might take up the question of judges' salaries. If this were a year in which the whole matter could
5 p.m. be discussed with fairness, I think the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) would be eminently right in the position he takes, not so much upon the ground that the Alberta judges will be envious, but upon the ground that so far as the judges' salaries are concerned, there should be no increase from this House unless the minister is going to deal with the whole question, which, manifestly he cannot do on account of the necessity of strict economy all round. I think that it is important, when the country is in a position to do it, that steps should be taken to provide ample salaries for a good judiciary.

A message was delivered by J. D. St. Denis Lemoine, Esquire, I.S.O., Serjeant-at-Arms of the Senate, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy of His Royal Highness the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the Chamber of the honourable the Senate.
