speechtext: The House resumed in Committee, Mr. Blain in the Chair, in consideration of the proposed resolution wiith respect to the salaries of judges in the province of Saskatchewan.

Instead of a Supreme Court, consisting of a Chief Justice and four puisne judges, the province of Saskatchewan now proposes to have a Court of Appeal composed of a Chief Justice and three puisne judges, and another court known as the Court of King's Bench, consisting of a Chief Justice and five puisne judges. In other words, there are now to be ten high court judges in that province. As the right hon. leader of the Opposition pointed out, under the constitution the determination as

to the number of judges and the manner of dealing with the cou'ts rest entirely with the Provincial Legislature. They have chosen to say:	We will require twice as
many high court judges as we now have. That will give in the province of Saskatchewan no less than twenty-seven judges, including the county court judges, whereas in the province of Nova Scotia, with the same population, we are getting along with thirteen judges altogether, or less than half as many.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Out in the West the people are more vigorous.
Probably so, but it seems to me they will have ample courts hereafter.
I am under the impression that quite a number of the county court judgeships have not been filled.

I take the figures
from the Estimates of this year, which provide for seventeen judges in Saskatchewan. Whether that is right or wrong, apparently in this Parliament we cannot question the action of the Provincial Legislature, so that it is only interesting to mention the matter by way of passing reference, so far as the consideration of this proposition is concerned, and my contention is that those judges who are to be taken from the Supreme Court as it now exists to the Appellate Court ought to be content, until the war is over, with the' same slaries as they have enjoyed heretofore. If the judges who are on the Supreme Court of Saskatchewan are to be promoted, in the ordinary sense of the word, to this Appellate tribunal, they will be rid of the trouble of going on circuit and they will have nothing to do except to sit at the central point where the full court holds its sittings and hear cases on appeal. I say to my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett), who puts forward the invidious distinction between those two provinces, that he does not put the case on the ground which we in this House ought to take, and which we can take in regard to this matter. When we consider, for instance, the economies practised by men in high positions in England, and when we realize that for the first time we are proposing direct taxation in Canada, and that that taxation must be increased before our war problems are settled, it seems to me clear that the gentlemen who are to be appointed to this tribunal should be content with $7,000 for

the chief justice and $6,000 for the puisne judges, until the war is over and matters adjust themselves. Under normal conditions, I am in favour of liberal compensation to men who occupy these high positions. I do not know what the policy of the Government is with regard to the appointment of judges to the appellate court, but in my judgment the judge in the appellate court should be a man who has had experience in the court of first instance. I think that every man who has had experience at the bar will agree that we are not imposing any hardship upon these gentlemen in this year of war conditions if we say to them: whatever we may do when we come to readjust salaries later on, in view of the special circumstances no extra salary will be given now. Of what use is it to talk economy to the people of this country, of what use is it to tell them from the public platform of the problems that face the Dominion, if in dealing with these gentlemen in high positions-estimable gentlemen as they are; my remarks aTe not made in any personal sense-we give them an extra thousand dollars all around just for luck. That is not the true position for this Parliament to take at the present juncture.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the point made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) is that we should level things down. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) thought that we should level things up.
They should be left as they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They cannot be left as they are with regard to a tribunal, the salaries for whose members have never been fixed. I could, level things down from what is usually given to judges of the courts of appeal-though I do not say that is applicable to all the provinces. As to the suggestion of the need for special economy just now, it is true economy is of the very greatest importance. But the economy suggested would be, for this year, a matter of $4,000. I think that hon. members generally will agree that when the salaries of judges of a province are once fixed it takes a tremendous force to alter them. It would therefore seem to be wise, when we are called upon to fix salaries as we are called, upon in this case, to so fix them that we may hope that it will be a considerable period of time before it will
be found necessary to do anything in the way of an increase. It does not seem to me that the economy to be effected by putting the judges of this Court of Appeal on a different footing from the judges of the Court of Appeal of the adjoining province of Manitoba, for instance-

How about New
Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It may be that we are profiting by our experience in the case of New Brunswick. If, when the Appellate Court of New Brunswick was constituted, the matter had been dealt with as it is proposed to deal with this, perhaps we should not have had the anomaly that exists in relation to the court in New Brunswick. But, as I said, in answer to the hon. member for Calgary, we have to deal with Saskatchewan to-day, and I think the wisest way is to deal with it in what we may call a permanent manner.

As to the comparison made by the hon. member for Pictou between Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia, even his figures, I think, woulc( not justify keeping the salaries in Saskatchewan at the same figure as those in Nova Scotia. Our judges in Saskatchewan are resident in a province where living is undoubtedly more expensive than in the province of Nova Scotia.
What proof is there of that?

All the data is to that effect, and I think there is no questioning the statement; I cannot speak from personal knowledge, as I have never been in Nova Scotia. As the Minister of Justice has said, the court is now being constituted and this is the time when the salaries have to be fixed on the merits of the case. The argument of leave well enough alone does not apply, because we are dealing with a new court in which the appointments have yet to be made. 'There is nothing on the record to show that the present members of the Saskatchewan Bench will be appointed to the Supreme Court, although some of them may be. The new appointments are to be made, and naturally we want the best men who can be obtained. The salaries must be fixed accordingly, which is altogether a different matter from increasing the salaries of men who have made a contract with the Government practically for life. It is only ordinary busi-

ness to say that the salaries should he made of sufficient magnitude to attract the best men. I do not wish to reflect on the money-making powers of members of the legal profession in Nova Scotia, but I suspect that the money-making power of those in Saskatchewan is greater. The cost of living is higher than in Nova Scotia. Consequently before you can hope to draw men away from a comparatively remunerative profession, you will have to make substantial provision for their emoluments in their new positions. I think that in the province of Saskatchewan the salary should be still more liberal. I see that we have five judges of appeal in Ontario, each of whom is paid $8,000 a year. The cost of living in Saskatchewan is higher than in Ontario-higher - for the judge and higher for his family. To educate his children he will probably have to send them away from home. If he takes a holiday, it is a matter involving great expense. There are a hundred ways in which I could illustrate the greater expense resting upon those who occupy judicial positions in Saskatchewan than on those in similar positions in Ontario. I have thought for ten or eleven years that members of Parliament from the West should be paid more than members from Ontario and Quebec, because we are away from home all the time, and have a longer distance to travel. I would move a resolution like that myself, but it would not be in order; it would have to obtain the approval of His Royal Highness in Council. What is the modus operandi of getting these appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I could tell something
about the modus operandi of giving them, but not about the modus operandi of getting them.

The Provincial Government has to make a proclamation approving the discontinuance of the old court, and on the passing of that proclamation the new court is brought into being. In connection with the new court, the Government has to make appointments. What I want to know is, which of these two steps is taken first?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My understanding of it was that before we should act at all, the Gbvemment of Saskatchewan should issue a proclamation fixing the time when their law should go into force, but the Government of the province of Saskatchewan would not proclaim their law until we first passed

a law providing for the salaries. For my part, I think that the proper administration of justice and the giving effect to this Act was more important than the punctilio as to whether we should step out first or whether the Government of Saskatchewan should step out first. Although I thought and still think that it belonged to them to step out first, I am stepping out first. I am providing that the Bill based on this resolution shall go into force only upon the law in Saskatchewan having been put into force by the Government of Saskatchewan, and thereirpon, by proclamation of the Governor in Council here establishing that fact. I hope that we shall get co-operation in that way to bring this law into effect.
I do not yet understand my hon. friend's answer. Do they make proclamation first, or does the minister make the appointments first?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Parliament cannot provide salaries for a court that does not exist; therefore, this legislation of ours can not be effective until the Government of Saskatchewan-I must' say in parenthesis that it looks as if it had a terrible hesitation about its own law-will choose to proclaim its own law, which is the condition of its coming into force. The moment that they are pleased to do that, we will bring this Act into force by proclamation here, and the judges will be appointed and the salaries provided. For my part, as long as we get the practical result of putting the law in operation, I am willing that the Government of Saskatchewan should step out first and that I should step out behind, or that I should step out first and let them step out behind.
I understand, then, that the Saskatchewan Government makes its proclamation creating the new courts, and the minister afterwards makes the appointments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Immediately upon the proclamation issuing by the province bringing the law into force; our proclamation will issue and appointments be made and salaries provided.
I do not think the explanation that the minister made with regard to bringing in the Bill naturally arose out of my question. I was not asking about the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought the hon. gentleman wanted the whole modus operandi; I did not know that he drew any

specific distinction between the future and the past.

If that is the minister's view, his answer was quite consistent with it. The minister has gone into the question of who should step out first and who should step out second in this procession. I may say that there went out to the Conservative press in Saskatchewan an account of an alleged interview between Hon. Walter Scott and the Solicitor General, and it was stated that in that interview there had been some conflict of opinion. Mr. Scott states, however, that there was no such conflict. He says that when he was in Ottawa he had an informal interview with the Solicitor General, and that he, Mr. Scott, took no particular stand as to his position on this point. The matter was one that did not come within Mr. Scott's department, and he gave absolute contradiction to the statement that he in any way had locked horns or joined issue with the Solicitor General or with the Government on the question as to who should step out first.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was not referring to any interview between the Solicitor General and Mr. Scott. I am not finding fault with the Saskatchewan Government because they have one view of what ought to he done and we have another. It was not my view that it was for us to act first, but I was willing to yield my opinion in that regard. It was very firmly indicated to me that the Government of Saskatchewan would not act until we did. That being so, and the matter being of not material importance, I was willing to let my opinion be passed over in order that the people of Saskatchewan might get the kind of court that, by their Legislature, they had said they wanted.	-

Up to about seven years ago, we had no district court judges in the province of Saskatchewan. When district courts were introduced which corresponded with the county courts in the older provinces, what procedure was followed? Who stepped out first then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not looked it up, and' I do not know:

I concur in the remarks made by the hon. member for Pictou to the effect that in these times, when economy is necessary, the salaries of these judges should not be increased. The judges who sit in the Supreme 'Court are just as well
qualified as those who sit in the Court of Appeal, and I do not see why there should be a difference in the salaries. A salary of $6,000 a year, or $500 a month, should be amply sufficient, having regard to the fact that the position is far life, and that generous provision is made in the way of retiring allowance.
The judges are better paid at $6,000 than ministers of the Crown are at $7,000, and they have nothing like the same expenses. I submit that the salaries of the judges of the Court of Appeal should be on the same plane as those of the Supreme Court. They require no greater knowledge of the law. Judges who go on circuit have less time to deliberate, and the cases come before them in less carefully prepared form than before the Court of Appeal. They really have to be better qualified than the judges who sit in appeal. There should be no difference; it creates jealousy and is invidious. The chief justices, of course, should receive higher salaries.
To my mind we have too many judges in this country.
Hear, hear.

The number ought to be greatly reduced, and a better system adopted by which we would have younger judges, who would, be paid better salaries. As I read the signs of the times, there will be a demand in this country, after the war, for a recasting of our whole system of jurisprudence, a simplification of the courts, and a speedier system of obtaining judgment, with fewer appeals from one court to another. Thus we could have fewer judges and pay them better salaries. The jurisprudence in Canada is altogether too elaborate, and is becoming more elaborate and more costly; more men are identified "with the administration of the law than would be required under a reformed system. In Great Britain to-day there is a general protest against the old system of jurisprudence, and especially against the undue influence of the legal profession upon the conduct of public business. The people of this country want a change; they want a simplification of the whole system of jurisprudence, they want quicker judgments and fewer appeals from judgments when they have been rendered. If that. reform is not worked out and we go on. increasing the number of officials, and the number of persons who have to be pensioned, a very emphatic demand will come from the public for a change.

Has the Minister of Justice gone into the question of the need of these appointments in Saskatchewan? I take it that this means the appointment of four additional judges at the increased salary. I have been under the impression that although the population and the area of Saskatchewan are larger than those of Alberta, still, owing toi the variety of business in Alberta, there is probably as much work for the courts in that province as in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not made any inquiry to ascertain how Saskatchewan compares with Alberta in that respect, but, as I have said, the necessity for this change has been very strongly impressed on me, and it has been urged, by the Attorney General of Saskatchewan, by those in the active practice of the profession, and by the judges who are administering justice that there was need for this reconstitution of the courts in order f-o secure . the proper expedition of public business. But, even if I thought this was not desirable, under the constitution, if any province determines that it needs this sort of machinery to carry on the administration of jurisprudence, it has, under the British North America Act, the power to determine that. It has control of the constitution of the courts, which involves the determination of how many courts and judges there shall be. In this particular instance, if we failed to meet this demand we would either compel Saskatchewan to go on with a system which its legislature, which has the power to determine the question, has decided is not suitable, or, if the Legislature brought its law into force, we would leave the province with no courts at all. So, while I have made some inquiry to satisfy myself that, at all events, there is evidence that it is not an unreasonable request, at the same time I am not an absolutely free agent to sit here and determine whether this change ought to he made or not. My belief, from information derived from what I believe to be reliable sources, is that there is justification for the desire for the additional number of judges and a better system of disposing of the public business.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

And the Estimates for 1916-17, in which there is a decrease, are $3,304,000. In the year 1910-11, when the department was conducting more than twice as much business as it is now, the cost of the department was less than half what it is now. There

has been a doubling of the cost and a cutting in half of the business. We are under war conditions and naturally there is a demand for a curtailment of expenditure. Reasons that might be given and that would be perfectly good for the maintenance of a certain scale of expenditure had peace conditions continued do not stand good today under war conditions. When we consider the enormously increased burdens that the country must necessarily bear as a result of war expenditure, in regard to which we have been informed by the. Minister of Finance and which we have reason to know because of the taxation proposals that he has put through, we understand that the call is for a greater exercise of economy than ever prevailed before instead of for a doubled expenditure in the face of the cutting in half of the requirements. Just on that point, let me read a quotation from the Premier of Great Britain that I think is apt to this case. A deputation had called upon Mr. Asquith protesting against the closing of the museums and art galleries which were under the control of the British Government. The reply of the Premier- and I commend it very strongly to all those who have responsibility in the management of the affairs of the country at the present time-was this:
In view of the stupendous and unprecedented liabilities and obligations which the war is imposing upon us, if we are, as I think we are still agreed that we are to subordinate every other purpose to its effectual and successful prosecution, one of the first means which prudence and policy prescribe in the attainment of that object is the temporary reduction of every form, both of public and of private expenditure, which can be shown not to be directly conducive to that purpose.
I cannot bring any higher authority in support of the view that I have expressed. I did not, however, wish to bring these facts before the committee merely in a fault-finding spirit; I wanted to impress upon the committee and upon the minister and the Government this fact, that, if money is spent for those purposes that are not essential and that can be dispensed with, it is not then available for expenditure on the purposes that are essential and that cannot, in the interest of the country, be dispensed with.
A great deal has been said in the newspapers and upon the public platforms as to what will occur at the close of the war, and, as I read these statements, there is a concensus of opinion that the future of Canada rests and will rest upon the increase of production from the land. War
CMr. Oliver. I
conditions seem to have brought home this idea more strongly to the minds of those writers and speakers than it ever was before. It is agreed then that we must look forward to the increase of agricultural production. In order to increase agricultural production, we must have labour applied to the land, and in order to get that labour applied to the land we must offer the conditions that will be attractive to labour, or otherwise we shall not get that increase of production upon which every one is agreed that the future of Canada is absolutely dependent. The experience of the past shows that the great factor in securing the agricultural development of the Canadian West, upon which development the industrial and commercial development of the rest of the country has depended in large measure, has been the attraction of free prairie land under conditions suitable for occupation and profitable production by the homesteader. The free prairie land of our western country has to a very large extent passed from the control of the Crown, having been alienated in one form or another. Any one who takes the trouble to look at one of the homestead maps issued by the Department of the Interior, in which the condition of settlement is very lucidly set forth, will see that that part of the western provinces which constitutes the great prairie area of the Red river and the Saskatchewan drainage basins, has been alienated, and therefore, so far as that area is concerned, we have no free land to offer to new settlers. The question then is: are our possibilities exhausted or have we further possibilities available; and, if so, in what direction and under what circumstances? Outside of that area which is already occupied, there is to the north a partially wooded area. I am going to speak now of the province that I represent and principally of my constituency which covers a large part of northern Alberta. In northern Alberta, adjoining that area which is already settled and which might be called purely prairie land, there is a vast territory of timbered or partially timbered country of good soil and favourable climatic conditions, and available for free homesteads, but not as attractive as the purely prairie area. The land is there available, but, being partially wooded country, the difficulties of access to all parts are stupendously greater than they are in the purely prairie areas where, under ordinary conditions in the summer time, a man could hitch up his team and drive

anywhere without road-making; whereas, in this wooded or partially wooded area, the settlement can go only slowly as roads are built and as accommodation is provided, and people cannot branch out a hundred or a hundred and fifty miles away from other settlements as they could on the open and cleared prairies. Beyond the prairies of the Saskatchewan lies the partially-timbered region of the Athabaska, of which I have been speaking, and beyond that lie the prairies of the Peace river. The Peace river prairies are not a continuous area like the prairies of the Saskatchewan. In the Peace river country there are true prairie [DOT] areas, hut there is also a great deal of land partly timbered. There is no continuous stretch of hundreds of miles of prairie in the Peace river country as there is in the Saskatchewan country. These prairie areas of the Peace river are recognized as being very productive, and they have already attracted a large settlement. People have passed through the timbered country of the Athabaska to the prairie areas of the Peace river, and have occupied some of these prairie areas under circumstances of very great difficulty. The prairies of the Peace river are from 300 to 400, or even 500, miles distant from the railroad centre of Edmonton. This means that, while men may push their way through into these distant prairie areas and establish themselves as pioneers, they cannot by any possibility become producers on any considerable scale that would add materially to the wealth of the country unless and until they have railroad communication. The partially-timbered regions lying between the Saskatchewan and the Athabaska, and this prairie areas of the Peace, are dependent upon railroad development for their full occupation to a very much greater degree than were the open prairie areas of the Saskatchewan country. The Government of Alberta has recognized the needs of the pioneers who have gone into this northern country, and, by guaranteeing the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway in some instances, and in other instances the railroad enterprises that are headed by one J. D. McArthur, it has been able to secure the construction of a very great mileage of railways. Trains are now running from Edmonton to Peace River Crossing, a distance of 310 miles. They are also running by a branch line from this line to Spirit River, a distance of 357 miles, and from Spirit River to Grand Prairie they are either running now or will be within a very few days, a distance 131
of fifty miles further, or a total distance from Edmonton of over 400 miles. To the north-easterly, the Waterways railroad has steel laid for a distance of 180 miles, and the grading is completed to Fort McMurray, a distance of 300 miles from Edmonton. These roads,- with one exception that I shall mention, are being constructed wholly on the guarantees of the Provincial Government; they have not cost the Dominion Government a cent, although the Provincial Government of Alberta has no responsibility in regard to the development of the province. The responsibility of the Provincial Government is to find accommodation for people who are there, but on the Dominion Government rests the responsibility of developing the natural resources of the province, because the Dominion Government owns the lands, the timber, and the minerals of Alberta, as it owns those of Saskatchewan and of Manitoba. This responsibility cannot by any process of reasoning be placed primarily upon the Provincial Government. Notwithstanding that fact, the Provincial Government has guaranteed railroad bonds for 400 miles from Edmonton to Grand Prairie, by way of Spirit river, and with a branch of 50 miles to Peace River crossing; also 300 miles on the Great Waterways railroad to Fort McMurray. These are the McArthur railway enterprises. The Provincial Government have also guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway for approximately 100 miles from Edmonton to Athabaska Landing, and from Edmonton north-easterly to a village called St. Paul de Metis, and north-westerly 130 miles to White Court. All these lines are in settled territory of the partially wooded character of which I spoke. 1	.
My reason for bringing this matter to the attention of the House at this time-and I am glad to see the Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) in his place -is this:	The Provincial Government
has gone as far as it can go -at least that would be my judgment-in the guaranteeing of these lines. These guarantees have produced magnificently great results up to the present time, but, unfortunately, it has not been possible up to the present moment to realize all the expectations that were entertained when the guarantees were given. Let me say, however, that I notice in the Estimates an item indicating that the Dominion Government propose to give a bonus of $6,400 a mile for that section of the Dunvegan rail-



way line from Spirit River to Grand Prairie. That, I think, is very proper, but that 50 miles is the only portion, of the whole length of about 1,000 miles that I have mentioned as having been guaranteed by the provincial government, towards which the Dominion Government will have contributed a cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman include in that 1,000 miles?

I gave the figures, but I
will repeat them, if I may:
Dunvegan railway, 400 miles to Grand Prairie-50 miles to be bonused by this Government; a branch from McLellan to Peace River Crossing, 50 miles. Waterways Railway: Edmonton to McMurray, approximately 300 miles. Canadian Northern: Athabaska line, approximately 100 miles, completed; the St. Paul de Metis branch of the Canadian Northern, 100 miles, only partly graded and none of it ironed. Peace River Branch to White Court, 130 miles, of which 66 miles to Sian Gudo, has the steel and the balance of the line graded. So, as a result of the provincial government's guarantee, we have 1,000 miles of railway completed or to be completed on provincial guarantees alone without any assistance whatever from the Federal Government.
We have 50 miles that is about completed with assistance from the Federal Government, and we have 230 miles of Canadian Northern that is incomplete at the present time. I do not wish to be considered as advocating the interests of the Canadian Northern Railway Company; I am here to advocate the interests of my constituents and of the pioneers in other sections of the country whose present and future is dependent on the early completion of these two branches. My contention is that if it is necessary to secure the completion of these branches by assistance from this Government over and above the guarantees given by the Provincial Government, it would be a very much wiser expenditure of the resources at the disposal of the Government than the expenditures that are asked for in the excessive Estimates that are now before the House. What I would urge is that, instead of the resources of the country being expended in the maintenance of a number of officials over and above those that are necessary for the business that is being done, the money be used to make sure that the partially or entirely wooded free-gramt country can be reached
TMr. Oliver.]
and developed by those who enter into it and undertake the tremendous labour of clearing it. At the present time the road for 100 miles northeast of Edmonton is incomplete, and about sixty miles of the road norhtwest from Edmonton is incomplete. It is absolutely urgent, in the interests of the settlers who are now in occupation of that country, to say nothing of the future development of the country, that these sections of the road be completed without delay, and I take this opportunity of bringing the matter as strongly as I can to the attention of the Government. I have drawn attention to what I consider the over-expenditure in the Interior Department, not for the purpose of finding fault, but for the purpose of suggesting to the Government that in making appropriations for the completion of these two necessary lines of railroad they would be conserving the country to very much greater advantage than they are at present by unnecessary expenditure in the Interior Department.

Is not the policy that my hon. friend advocates entirely contrary to that which is being developed the world over, namely, the intensive treatment of agriculture? Does he think it wise that population should run all over the face of the earth, dragging railways after it and pushing them ahead of it, instead of settling within reasonable areas and cultivating rapidly and properly a country. which can be reached much more easily and at less expense?

I am strongly in favour of that system, which in ten or fifteen years, brought Canada from the end of the procession to the head of the procession. That was the policy of throwing the land wide open and of giving to the man who wanted to use it every facility for taking it up. I am not an advocate of what my hon. friend calls the intensive cultivation of land as our means of securing national prosperity. My idea is to bring into production the vast areas of land that are now producing nothing, even if that production should not be absolutely up to the standard of the intensive cultivation that my hon. friend has in his mind. The good results to the country at large will be achieved by bringing as many people into as strenuous activity as possible, and you can do that best by offering to them the reward of free land for their enterprise.
I have spoken of the railroad lines running northeast and northwest from Edmon-

ton. I want to speak of two further ex tensions of the Dunvegan line that I consider are very necessary to the welfare, of the people immediately concerned, and would be enormously helpful to the further development of the country. From Spirit river the distance to the boundary between Alberta and British Columbia is some sixty miles, and beyond the boundary is what is called the Poucg Coups prairie, an area of four or five townships of prairie which are already occupied by settlers. This is a part of what is called the Peace river block, an area of 3,500,000 acres. It is within the province of British Columbia on both sides of the Peace river, but it is the property of this Government. The Government of Canada has assumed ownership of it and is responsible for its development.
This Pouce Coupe prairie is not withm the province of Alberta, and therefore is not in any way under the control of. the Alberta Government. However, the Government of Alberta has guaranteed the bonds of the Dunvegan railway from Spirit river to the provincial boundary. Every one knows that you cannot raise grain, or do a farming business, sixty miles from a railway through a wooded country and make money or secure any considerable development. I do not know whether the railway company will be able to make that extension or not on the provincial guarantee, but if they are not able to do it on the provincial guarantee I submit that this Government may fairly and properly come to the assistance of the company with the ordinary railway bonus. The other location that I wish to speak of is on the north side of the Peace river, extending from Peace river, crossing westerly to a point opposite Dunvegan, a distance of sixty miles. I visited that particular part of the country last spring, and I would say that there is no other area in the prairie West that is of equally good, quality throughout as that stretch of sixty miles from Peace river crossing to Dunvegan on the north side of the Peace river. This stretch of country, which is from fifteen to twenty miles wide, and runs from the river northward, is already occupied by a most energetic and enterprising class of people. The improvements that they have mad(e there are simply remarkable, in view of the difficulties that they have had in reaohing that country before the completion of the railroad. When the railroad is completed as it is now to Peace river crossing, these people will have to haul their grain 10, 15, 13H
20, 30, 40, 50, or 60 miles, as the case may be, to the railroad, and in doing so will have to descend into the Peace river valley, a depth of some 800 feet, besides crossing a river some 2,000 feet wide. It is true that these people are carrying on business there, and that it is a prairie area, so that the roads are fairly good. But if that area, and that which lies beyond on the north side of the river for a distance of 200 miles from the crossing-to Hudson's Hope, are to be developed, the railroad must be carried across the river and out of the valley up to the upland and along that upland for some distance. The Provincial Government has given a guarantee of bonds that would cover the railroad for some 50 miles beyond the crossing, but, even if the bonds could be sold, that guarantee would not be sufficient to cover the enormous cost of carrying the railroad out of the valley, a depth of 800 feet. If that settlement on the north side of the Peace river is to get railroad communication, and if the country beyond, which is equally good although not yet settled, is to be developed by railroad, that railroad must be extended across the river and out of the valley up to the upland. I am speaking on this occasion without authority from the Provincial Government or from either of the railroad companies concerned. I am not interested in either one or the other; but I am interested in the development of the country of which I speak, and which I have the honour to represent in this House. I am sure that the country at large is as much interested as I am, and it is the business of the Government to be interested in it also. T; 5 settlers who are there are in need of relief such as I have spoken of as a result of the Provincial Government's guarantee; but the further development of the Peace river country must depend on further extension of railroad communication, and I place before this Government on this occasion this argument, that it is upon their shoulders, and not upon the shoulders of the Provincial Government, that the responsibility for the development of that country rests.
To repeat my argument, I consider that the expenditures which are being made by the Department of the Interior at this time, considering the amount of business transacted, are abnormal. In order to bring the business of the country up to normal again, further railroad extensions will have to be made. I am placing the facts as I understand them before the Government for their best consideration.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A good deal of the criticism that has been offered by the exMinister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) has nothing whatever to do with the item under discussion, or with the department over which I have the honour to preside. However, I am sure the House has listened with great interest to his remarks touching this country, a greater portion of which he has the honour .to represent, and its needs and requirements. I quite agree with him that ' it cannot be expected that that part of the country can be settled without adequate railway transportation facilities, and I think he himself afforded the key, in a portion of his argument, to the reason why the homestead entries have fallen off to some extent. We cannot expect the homestead entries to be maintained at the level of a few years ago, when practically all free land south of the latitude of the city of Edmonton has been taken up, so that settlers desiring homesteads now have to go many miles away from transportation facilities. It is not much inducement to settlers to go into a remote country when if they do raise crops they have no tran .-por'tation facilities to convey them to the market so that their raising of crops would prove most unremunerative. However, when the hon. gentleman speaks of the necessity of this Government taking into, consideration the subsidizing of certain branch lines of railway in that country, that is something with which I am personally not very conversant. I am nothin a position to state whether or not it is the intention of the 'Government to bring down any railway subsidies, but, in so far as this particular portion of the country is concerned, there. is an item in the Estimates, to which the hon. member has referred, by which it is shown that the Government is recognizing the necessity for transportation facilities in that part of the country and is subsidizing, to the extent of $6,400 a mile for a certain mileage, in that country. I take issue with the hon. gentleman when he states that the cost of administering the' Department of the Interior is . double what it was a few years ago, whereas the business of the department has practically been cut in -two. It is all right enough to take up the Estimates of a certain year, say .1910-11, and compare them with those for 1915-16 and say that the expenditure under the head of Dominion Lands, for instance, has increased by $1,000,000 or $2,000,000. In order to have a 
fair comparison, you must look into the details. There are items under these heads for 1915-16 which were not included under the same headings when the hon. gentleman was minister. There is upwards of $1,000,000 in the Estimates for the present year that were not included in 1911, that was voted under other heads. For instance certain items that are now included under Dominion Lands and Parks were placed in 1910-11 under miscellaneous.
What items?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Take the Parks Branch,
which was established only a few years ago. Then there are a number of other items the necessity for which have arisen since 1910-11.

I think the Dominion
Parks were included in 1911.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes, 1911 was the first
year they were included. The following items which are voted under Dominion Lands and Parks for 1914-15 were voted under miscellaneous for 1910-11 or are votes for services the necessity of which has arisen in the past few years. Take, for instance, Canadian National Parks. In the year 1914-15 the vote was $649,630. I have cut that almost in two for the present year, and there was voted under this head $349,000 instead of $649,000, a reduction for this year of some $300,000 in connection with parks. Then, again, there was the printing and engraving of maps, $78,000. That was included under miscellaneous in 191011. Then there 'is the cost of litigation and legal expenses, $11,000. Then we have an item in the past year, irrigation $40,000 and Southern Alberta Land Company, refund, $190,000; relief to the town of Frank, etc. Thus we have a number of items, which go to make up a sum total of upwards of $1,000,000, which were voted under other headings when the hon. gentleman was Miuister of the Department. When the ex-minister states that the. homestead entries afford a very good index as to the business being done in the department and the necessity for so large a number of officials, my views do not harmonize with his in this respect either. We must realize that, while the homestead entries afford a very good index as to the number of people going upon the land, it does not necessarily follow that they afford an index of the business done in the various land offices. As a matter of fact, the taking of patents involves very much more work than the

taking of applications for homestead entry, and protests come in sometimes from men who have put in applications for patents which cause reference back to files, and considerable correspondence with the various agencies and sub-agencies and necessitates, on many occasions, as the hon. gentleman well knows, special inspection on the part of the homestead inspectors. He will see by looking at the list of applications for patents that the number of patents issued has kept up very well indeed, and that they have not fallen off like the applications for homestead entries.
They have fallen off some.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Very little. Even if the homestead entries and applications for patents fall off, should we disorganize our service by dismissing officials from the various land agencies? There is other work for them to do, and, besides, it would prove a hardship to those men who have families dependent upon them to dismiss them as soon as business falls off. That is not what the ordinary business man does, and it is less the practice in the Government service.
I would ask my hon. friend's attention to one point, in connection with those officials, which he has overlooked entirely. The item is for the salaries of the outside service. From the outside service of the Department of the Interior there have enlisted up to date upwards of 160 officials. That is quite a drain upon the outside service, and, as we have, to pay them their salaries while they are absent, the expenditure keeps up just the same. One hundred and sixty officials of the outside service have enlisted, and in addition there is a number of pending applications.
Has my hon. friend not got along without them?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Quite a large number of other applications for leave of absence for the purpose of enlisting have been before the department, and they have not been favourably passed upon up to date by reason of the fact that our agents in the West report that they cannot get along without substitutes. I was going to say before my hon. friend interrupted me that out of , the 160 who have enlisted, we have replaced only 40, leaving about 120 whose places have not [DOT]been filled. We are getting along 9 p.m. without them by doubling up the work; it is better to do that
than to dismiss men when the work falls off. It is one thing to double up the work, and another to dispense with the services of men once they are in the Government employ. My hon. friend has had sufficient experience of the working of the department to know that it is very much easier to increase the staff than to reduce it.. Once men are on the permanent staff, even although the work does fall off, it does not always follow that dismissals should take place right and left.
There are several branches of the Interior Department for whose establishment I am not responsible. I am not offering any adverse criticism of the minister who preceded me because he made them separate branches. There are the Forestry Branch, the Irrigation Branch and the Water-powers Branch; they have their various heads and staffs whose work has been of a most important character and has developed to a very great extent during the ,last few years. Take the Forestry Branch; we have enlarged our forestry work, not as one hon. gentleman suggested a few nights ago for the purpose of creating officials, because it was done on the representation of the head of the Forestry Branch, and not on my own initiative. From time to time there have been added to the forestry reserves large additional areas. Four or five years ago, I think there were somewhere in the neighbourhood of 3,000,000 acres, and these reserves have been increased to 23,000,000 acres. The forestry service requires a staff to properly safeguard the forest wealth of the country. We all recognize the devastation that has taken place, particularly in Western Canada, as the result of fire. If we were to follow out the recommendations made by the Conservation' Commission, the Lumbermen's Association, and the General Forestry Association of the Dominion I would have to ask Parliament to vote considerably larger amounts of money than I do at the present time. I have tried to keep pace with what I think are the requirements of the country with the view of securing better fire protection for our large timber areas in the West. Then, although we have a large number of forestry officials, we have not anything like the number that there is in the province of Ontario. There are large areas to control in that western country, and those hon. gentlemen who have read the reports of the destruction that has taken place during the past twenty-five years will realize what a national asset our timber reserves are. and

how careful we should be to see they are not devastated by fire.
In addition, we have, in connection with the Interior Department, created new land districts, and new land offices. We have opened, I think, four at Revelstoke, Wey-burm, Maple Creek and Peace River. These all required additional staffs. We have increased not only the land agencies but also the sub-agencies. In the northern portion of the country, where distances are great, the settlers are averse to travelling 100 or 200 miles to make an entry, or prove a claim, and we have endeavoured to keep up with the requirements by placing subagencies where the conditions did not warrant the establishment of agencies. Of course, it is very much more expensive to establish a Dominion land agency than it is to establish a sub-agency, but 'the multiplication of these sub-agencies have increased the number of officials materially in connection with the administration of the affairs of the department.
There are many things of that nature that I might refer to. Take our ranch regulations. We toad, a ranch commission, which reported a ferw years ago, and which recommended that we should inaugurate new ranch regulations. I think the old regulations applied only to lands south of Township 44, or thereabouts, but under the new regulations they apply all over the three western prairie provinces where lands have been pronounced unsuitable for agriculture, and they have necessitated the appointment of additional ranch inspectors.
Then we have opened up a new forest products laboratory in the city of Montreal, in connection with the forestry branch of the department. I venture to say that comparatively few members of this House are aware of the fact that during the past two or three years we have been conducting a forest products laboratory in connection with McGill University, and if any hon. members would visit McGill University and see the work that is being done there under the auspices of the forest products laboratory, they would be filled with pride I am .sure. I was surprised myself at the official opening some months ago, to see the splendid work that is being carried on there. That entailed alone the addition of some forty employees. The laboratory was established not to. give employment to political supporters. As a matter of fact, merit is the qualification for the appointments. We appointed experts, men who were recommended by the head of the branch,
fMr. Roche.]
and we did not allow politics to play any part in the appointments whatever.
If there are any other questions that hon. members would like to ask, I am quite prepared to. answer them, or, if the Acting Minister of Railways desires to say anything on the railway situation, I will give way to him. Notwithstanding the fact that the staff .has increased, we are asking for a smaller amount this year than last. I do not think that, under all the circumstances, much as we would all like to economize in this time of stress, I would be justified in reducing to any extent the salaries or the number of officials under present conditions.

In spite of all the explanations that the minister has given with regard to the continued increase in the cost of running this department, and while there may be one or two items in the vote that were not there five years ago when this Government came into power, the fact remains that the cost of running the Interior Department has practically doubled. As my hon. friend from Edmonton has pointed out, the amount of work done has been very greatly reduced. I quite agree with the minister that the cutting in two of the homestead entries would not mean the cutting in two of the work of the department. Nobody would expect my hon. friend to cut the staff in two simply because the entries have been cut down so much, but, while we have had a falling off during the last two or three years in the amount of work, and while this falling off would indicate that a smaller staff would be able to do the work, and that the department could get along very well with a smaller expenditure, we have the expenditure practically doubled. My hon. friend referred to the fact that he had opened new land offices, and that this always means expense. I am very well aware of the fact that the opening of new land offices increases the yearly expense, and I also know that in some of the northern parts of the country there is no doubt that new land districts are necessary when a new country is brought under settlement. But for every land office that my hon. friend opens up in the northern part of the country, he could close an office in the southern or older settled parts, where so many land offices are unnecessary. In my own constituency the land district was divided, and two land offices w^re established when there was no necessity for a new land office. It was a political job. The second land office was established for

the purpose of carrying out a political scheme and to give employment to a few officials. "Under the present war conditions my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), in putting new taxes upon the people, and these are absolutely necessary if no retrenchment is made. If there is to be no economy in the expenditure of the Government, these taxes are necessary. If there is to be no retrenchment additional taxes will be necessary. If the Department of the Interior, and other departments, would reduce their expenditure to what it was four years before, when the Government came into office, a great part of the taxes that are being put on the people would not be necessary. There is no reason why it should cost almost double to run the department as compared with what it cost ,four years ago, especially in view of the fact that the amount of business done is a great deal less now than it was then. The cost is altogether too high. While there may be some difficulty in reducing the cost, if an effort was put forth, there is no doubt that considerable progress could be made. It appears that the minister thinks that if he keeps the cost from going beyond what it was during the previous year he is doing well. If the minister had practised that for the last four or five years the expenditure this year would be very little over half what it is. But my hon. friend did not do that. The -expenses have gone on piling up year after year and this year, in spite of the war, in spite of the new taxes, the minister is making very little attempt to cut down expenditure. My hon. friend referred to the fact that 120 men have enlisted and have not been replaced. That shows that they can get along very well without these men. Whilst it is a very nice thing to be able to give employment to people who ask for it, it is hardly fair that the country should be taxed simply for the purpose of giving employment to people for whom there is not sufficient work. We have, in this item, a number of very large expenditures and I am sure that the minister could cut them down materially without interfering with the public service, help out the economy his colleague, the Minister of Finance is always talking about and enable him to get along without taxing the people to the extent that he now proposes to do.

Would the minister be good enough to give me some information in reference to the Forest Protection Department? He says that the Government have now 23,000,000 acres under the control of the Forestry Branch and that there have been a large number of enlistments from that branch. To my mind the Forestry Branch is a very important one and if the department does not keep up the work in connection with the prevention of forest fires it would be a very grave error. I would like to know if the branch has suffered from the enlistment of that number of men.
Mr. ROdHE: Twenty-two in the Forestry Branch, outside service, have enlisted.
What is the method oi guarding against fires?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have the country divided into fire areas, all in charge of a chief ranger who has a staff of forest rangers under him. There is a supervisor for each forest reserve and there are forest rangers on these reserves. Each one has his location upon the reserve and resides upon it. They have methods of communication by means of telegraph lines, look-out stations, and so on, they are supposed to patrol their beats every day and they keep a memorandum of where they are and what they are doing each day which is submitted to their chief at the end of each month.
Is there a space around these forest reservese cut out, or ploughed, in order to guard against fire?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In some cases but not in all.

I noticed that in the Elk Park reserve, near Lamont, a certain amount of this work had been done but apparently it had not been done systematically. A road was cleared to a certain extent and a little ploughing done, but not to my mind in such a way as to prevent a fire from getting in there. The importance of having these reserves properly protected so that they will be of value at some future time is very great; and, while I am inclined to think there have been no serious losses up to the present time, yet one can never tell -when a very serious fire might occur in a place as close to that settlement as Elk Park.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is a park, not a forest reserve.
But the same regulations govern both?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Much the same, but there is noT quite so much fire protection in regard to parks.

My hon. friend said that economy was exercised in the protection of the forests. Now, he must have been a party to and' had full knowledge of a Bill that is now before the House in the name of the Finance Minister designed to discourage the railways from protecting the forests through which they run. The Canadian Pacific Railway, at an expense of something like $600,000, prepared its motive power for the use of fuel oil; the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway remodelled its motive power in the same way; but the Government of which my hon. friend is a member has a Bill before the House for the purpose of taxing fuel oil. The object of that Bill, which was explained fairly well, was to encourage the use of coal and discourage the use of fuel oil. Now, it seems strange that one branch of the Government is ask. ing us to vote them a large sum of money to protect the forests and another branch of the Government is bringing in a Bill to discourage the use of fuel oil, which the railways were asked to use for the protection of the forests. In a memorandum which I have seen, it is stated that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, not on the order, but at the suggestion of the Board of Railway Commissioner 3, and at the suggestion of the Government of British Columbia, substituted fuel oil for coal. After they have done that along the line which my hon. friend has suggested for the protection of the forests, he is assisting a colleague to tax them for doing so and to discourage them at a certain rate per gallon. Fuel oil will now cost a very large sum of money, and, if these two companies find it less expensive to go back to the use of coal, as is hoped at least by the people in the coal business, then my hon. friend will find that by his own act he has prevented the protection of forests.
Might I ask the hon. member if he is of the opinion that the use of fuel oil is the only method by which the forests may be protected?

It is the best
method.

Not the only one, but ' the one which the Government of British Columbia and the Board of Railway Commissioners suggested to those railways, and,

of course, they must have had some evidence before them in order to arrive at that decision. Enough timber has been destroyed in Canada by sparks from the smoke stacks of locomotives burning coal to build up almost as many railways as we have in Canada at present. One of the great problems before this country for some years has been to protect the forests, not only during railway construction, which is a very dangerous period, but during the operation of the railways. During the construction of the Transcontinental through the forests of the Maritime Provinces an arrangement was arrived at between the Provincial Governments and the Federal Government by which its right of way was patrolled and guarded most carefully in order to protect the forests, and very little, if any, fire occurred. When I was Minister _ of Railways, complaint was made to me time after time by the people of British Columbia that there was danger of fire in the forests of that province owing to the operation of the railways. That problem was impressed upon the present Government of British Columbia; it was impressed upon the Government of Sir Richard McBride, because I am informed that his Government intimated to the railways that it would be in the interest of the province if they could see their way clear to introduce the use of fuel oil as a locomotive power. I am only calling the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior to the fact that, while on the one hand he is asking for money to protect the forests, on the other hand he is assisting in passing a Bill which is contrary to the protection of the forests.

Last year I called
the attention of the minister to the case of some settlers west of Wetaskiwin in connection with some lands that had timber on them and to which they had been granted homestead entry by the Department of the Interior. The patents have been held up for quite a long time now, and I am informed that as yet nothing has been done, although last year the minister promised that he would look very carefully into the case, and I believe he did send out some special inspectors to report upon it so that he could adjudicate upon the question. I do not wish to cast any reflection upon any party interested in this matter, but it is my absolute conviction that it is nothing but a matter of political patronage in the district of Wetaskiwin that is holding up this case. I had hoped that the minister

would be inclined to adjust this case without having to be at the beck and call of every inspector in that district. From my personal knowledge of the case, a great deal of political patronage has been injected into the matter. I trust the minister has done something to adjust the grievances of the settlers in that western district.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
To show how astray the
hon. gentleman is in his facts, it is only necessary for me to say that I have fulfilled the promise which I made to him last session. I had two independent timber rangers visit the particular district which he desired me to have inspected and reported upon. Notwithstanding the fact that those rangers handed in a report stating that those gentlemen had made an entry, I must say, in contravention of the laws of the country, because, although they had to make a declaration that there were twenty-five or less acres of timber on a quarter section, it turned out in many instances that there were 75 acres, 60 acres and so on; notwithstanding the fact that those timber inspectors recommended that those gentlemen get patents on the condition that we would survey out 25 acres, allowing them to select their own 25 acres, and that we would throw the surplusage of the timber open to permits for adjoining settlers, we recognized that there would be some little difficulty in carrying out that scheme, and some time ago I gave instructions for patents to issue to the very gentlemen to whom the hon. member desired to have patents issue.
Thank you.

Might I ask the minister if he has any scheme of reforestation apart from the protection of forests, or whether any experiments are being carried on?
which we hope is going to be a very important part of our forestry branch. The demand for these trees is increasing year by year. In addition, there is to be inaugurated a work of re-foresting many of the areas in the forest reserve that have been burned over.

Yes.
Mr., ROCHE:	Under the Forestry Act
we have a large number of trees which are being distributed in increasing numbers of recent years to the farmers who apply for them. I think there were 4,000,000 trees ready for distribution last year and there are about 5,000,<XK) for the present year. So large has been the demand for those trees from our Experimental Farm at Indian- Head that we have had to establish another nursery, and that is another reason why the expenditure has been increased. In a place called Sutherland, near the town in which my hon. friend resides, we have established another nursery which is only in its infancy as yet, but
Is there one at Vermilion?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Is there one at Hudson Hope or St. John?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Instructions have been
given to open one next month at St. John.

Is there one at Pouce
Coupe Prairie?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, the office was established there less than a year ago.

There is an estimate
here for engraving and lithographing.

Would the cost of the atlas come out of that item ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Could the minister tell me the cost of the atlas?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The atlas is not meant for general distribution but for distribution to universities, colleges and high schools, and to parliamentary representatives and other public men. We are selling it to outside parties at the bare cost of printing and binding, which, I believe, is about $3.

This being the last
item to be considered, I suppose it was understood that all other items might be discussed on this?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There was no understanding of that kind, but I have no objection.
PUGSLEY:	I had not the opportunity of being here all evening, and if the ' minister has explained the point I wish to ask about I will not trouble him to repeat. This item is for salaries of the outside service, the amount being $465,000, the same amount as last year. That strikes me as rather extraordinary in view of the statement made by the minister that a good many young men in this service had enlisted for the war.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The item is to pay salaries of timber inspectors, homestead inspectors, inspectors of land agencies, Dominion land and Crown timber sub-agencies, and so on. There are quite a number of these offices in Western Canada. I think I explained practically what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugs-ley) is asking about before he came in.
Did the minister explain why the same amount is asked for as last year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

Perhaps the minister
would state, without going into details, if fewer men are expected to be employed during the coming year than in the current year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have not made up our minds to dispense with the services of any of our permanent staff, especially in view of the fact that 160 have enlisted, of whom only 40 have been replaced. We pay the salaries of those who have enlisted. There have also been a number of applications before the department for leave of absence, for which we have not as yet given 
our sanction, because of the representations made by the superior officers of the applicants that their places would have to be filled in the event of their being allowed to go-a pretty good indication that we cannot get on without them.

The minister is carrying on the department as if there were no war in existence or even dreamed of. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) recently, in a very able speech in this House, argued very strongly that every public interest and every private interest should be subservient to the war, that we should realize that this is the first and greatest business in which Canada should engage. The minister tells us that 160 young men, whose salaries are covered by this item, have enlisted, and that he has filled the places of 40 of them at all events. It does seem to me there might be some economy in this department while the war is on.
The Finance Minister told us that while he was asking us for the very large sum of $190,000,000 for the coming year, the different ministers had actually had printed in the Estimates the enormous sum of $29,000,000, which the exigencies of the public service would not require to be expended during the coming year. But when the different items' of the Estimates are under consideration we are denied information.
I d,o not think that we are being fairly treated by the different members of the Government. The hon. Minister of the Interior tells us that many young men of his department want to enlist. Why do they want to enlist? Because the Empire demands their services; demands that they should make the supreme sacrifice that every loyal citizen who is capable of going to the front feels that he ought to make. Yet the minister coolly tells the committee that he declines to let them go.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I did not say anything of the kind.
Upon the report of their superior officers he has declined to let them go.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is quite wrong.
Then what did my hon. friend say?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I said that these applications were still pending. I did not say that I had declined to let them go.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not to my knowledge-that is, for this particular item.
Speaking generally of the minister's Estimates, will there by any supplementaries for the- coming year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not to my knowledge. There may be some that I am not aware of at the present time, but if there are any they will be comparatively small.

The hon. member for St. John was good enough to make a passing reference to myself. I feel quite certain that were it any place other than Parliament, and were it any person other than the distinguished member for St. John, most members of this committee would say that he had embarked upon what we call in common parlance a leg-pulling expedition. But I do not think the minister or any one else proposes to suffer any leg-pulling through the medium of any such observations as those which have just been made by my hon. friend. If he had been in the House he would have heard the former Minister of the Interior discuss with much care and not at undue length the very matters about which that hon. gentleman has a far wider and more correct knowledge than the hon. member for St. John. But with that desire which is always manifested by my hon. friend, to seem to have a working knowledge of everything and a. particular knowledge of nothing, he insisted upon embarking upon the discussion of an item which might have been fully explained to him had he been here and heard the hon. member for Edmonton. What are the facts? The fact is that 160 men enlisted, and 40 men only have taken their places and are doing the work they did before as well as the work of the 120 men who have gone. An Order in Council was passed providing that the salaries of these men as civil servants should be paid. If the bon. gentleman objected to the policy of the department by which it was agreed that the salaries of these men should be paid while they were on active service, the time and place for him to have talked was some two years ago. I suppose he does now object to these men receiving their pay; he prefers that they should not be paid by the State while serving the Empire of which he talks so glibly. Well, the Government concluded to pay them, and I have not heard any gentleman here make any complaint in that respect. The Order in Council was subsequently amended, so that the

amount paid is now the difference between the military pay of the individual in question and the amount which he was receiving in civil life while he was in the employ of the Crown. It does not seem to me that that is a very serious matter. It would' follow almost from necessity that if the same staff is being paid there would not be very much diminution in the Estimates for their payment, especially in view of the fact that 160 of them are not here and that 40 men have been taken on to do the work of that 160. There is nothing serious about that. When my hon. friend talks about the necessity for economy, he would in this item at least question the policy which allows men on active service to receive the pay that they were receiving before they enlisted. If I remember rightly the hon. member for Edmonton did not dispute the soundness of that policy. It does seem to me to come with ill grace from the hon. member from St. John at this time, after nearly two years of war, to question the policy of the Administration that provides that a man who was the servant of the Crown, at a compensation which was none too large, and is now serving the Crown in another capacity, risking his life, shall be paid what he received in civil life, or the difference between that and what he received as a military man.

Does that apply to all
men who have enlisted?

My understanding of the Order in Council is that all those who were employed as servants of the Crown and who enlisted when the war broke out continued to receive the pay that they- were receiving as in civil life. Later, when it was found that the number of men enlisted was much larger than was originally contemplated, the Order in Council was amended to provide that they should receive the difference between what they re-cived in civil life and their military pay.

Could my hon. friend
say how many enlisted before the 1st of November last and how many after?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think over 100 out of the 160 enlisted before the 1st of November.

I have been over the
three western provinces a good deal in the last two years, at the points where the Interior Department officials are mostly employed, and I do not think any man in this House who would see their daily grind would not say that they had plenty to do.

The seed grain and relief work added materially to the work of the servants of the Crown, so far as Calgary, Edmonton, and I think probably Saskatoon and other land offices throughout the West are concerned. As the minister explained, new land offices are being opened up in the country north of Edmonton, owing to the extension of railroads in that territory.
And in the south also for political purposes.
My friend says the railways are being opened up for political purposes.
No, land offices.
I beg his pardon, I had not heard of anything like that-in the locality 'in which I live-in southern Alberta. Perhaps my hon. friend has' wider knowledge than I have.

I am only speaking of
my own quarter.

It may be that in the
locality to which my hon. friend belongs it may have been necessary to open a few land offices in districts which had been neglected by the late Government. Looking over the list of land offices, I am bound to say that the difference between the number under the late Administration and the number under this Administration is not very great, and we have had the development of the north country in which I understood the hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) to say it would not be out of place to have a few more offices opened. As to the salaries of the officials, in my judgment they are underpaid, even in war times. This relates particularly to the junior clerks. Many of these receive only $48 a month. Such a salary is wholly incommensurate with* the duties devolving upon these officials. I think it is as much our duty in war times to take care of the people in our own country and give them a reasonable wage to live on, as it is to provide suitable food and clothing for those at the front. Many of the employees of the Department of the Interior in the West are inadequately paid. I have discussed this matter with the minister on several occasions, but he says it is impossible to increase salaries in war time, and I had to accede to his views. I do not believe that any more hard-working and efficient men and women are to be found in any department than are scattered through the West

in the inside and outside service of the Department of the Interior. Homestead inspectors who discharge arduous duties in travelling through the country in all kinds of weather to inspect homesteads, are certainly not overpaid at $100 a month. I desire to make these observations in fairness to the men and women employed in the service of the department in the West. The greatest complaint I have heard against the administration of the Department of the Interior is that, too many of the appointees of the late Administration have been permitted to retain their positions and draw their salaries, despite the fact that during the term of office of the Tate Administration they were very bitter and offensive partisans. No charges have been-definitely made against them and so the matter has not been proceeded with; but if there is any complaint it is more largely against those who served the Crown before 1911 than those who have served it since.

I am sorry if I have
taken up any time in asking about a matter in respect of which the hon. member for Calgary is perfectly satisfied.

So is the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver).
Mr. PTJGS'LEY: I have not heard any expression of satisfaction on his part.
You were not here for that.

All I have is a guarantee of the hon. member for Calgary that he is thoroughly and entirely satisfied, that his only complaint is that the expenditure is not greater.
