I was not speaking of the salaries paid to civil servants in the West who are doing work for the public; what I was complaining of was that in these very hard times, which began not concurrently witfi the war but shortly after this Government came into power and whicn resulted in a great falling off in immigration, a falling off which began within a year of the advent of this Government to power-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman quite right in his facts?
Yes, about 1913.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In the fiscal year ending 1913 we had the largest immigration in the history of Canada, that is 402,000 people. Up until a few months prior to the opening of the war, that is the fiscal year ending March 31, 1914, we bad 385,000 immigrants, so there was a very small falling off.

That was a considerable falling off, and my hon. friend knows perfectly well that a wave of depression was flowing over the whole Northwest at least "a year before the war began. He has only to take the statements of the presidents of the different banks, including Sir Edmund Osier, a prominent member of this House and president of the Dominion bank, that the war was in no way responsible for the hard times. Anybody who realizes what is taking place in this country to-day must admit that had it not been for the war and the stimulus that has been given by orders by the British Government for munitions of war and other war supplies in this country, the depression would have been very great indeed, as compared with what it is now. What I contend is that, our immigration having fallen off from upwards of 400,000 down to about 40,000, we do not require the same number of employees in the Department of the Interior as would be required if the immigration was as large as in previous years. That is the argument which I make and it has not been answered. The figures presented to the committee by the Minister of the Interior necessarily make us keep in mind not only the large expenditure in his department but the large expenditures in all the departments of the Government, the total of which to-day is pretty nearly double what it was within two or three years of the late Government going out of power.
Nonsense.
No, it is not nonsense. Take the Public Works alone.
You said all the departments.

Take the total expenditure for 1908 and compare it with the expenditure for the present year. I have not the exact figures, but I venture to say that the expenditure is about double for the coming year what it was in 1908, when the country was in the high tide of prosperity, and was going ahead by leaps and bounds. That is something to make every well-wisher of his country despair for the efficient administration of the affairs of the country by the Government which is now in power. We have to criticise these dif-
20M

ferent items, and I will venture to criticise them, notwithstanding the statement of my hon. friend from Calgary that I am seeking to pull the minister's leg. I have no idea of pulling the leg of the Minister of the Interior. What I desire to do is to pull back to the treasury of this country some of the money which he proposes to take out of it, and to keep in the pockets of the taxpayer some of the money which he purposes distributing among his officials whom he proposes to continue to employ during the coming year. What about the policy of the Government in paying the civil servants their full salary while they are in the service of the Empire? I will tell my hon. friend what I think about that. I think that the proper policy to adopt is to deduct from5 their salaries the pay which they receive as privates or officers.

That is what is
being done now.

That is what the Government ought to have done in the first place, but the Opposition were not consulted about that matter any more than they were consulted about other matters in connection with the war. This Government has taken upon itself the Whole responsibility. It has done things which my hon. friend must admit were wrong, and which the Government itself admitted were wrong when they passed the Order in Council in November last. They did those things without thought. Even to-day, I venture to say that the minister cannot tell me whether the officials of his department Who have gone into the Government service since the war began will be permitted to enlist and will receive their salaries the same as the officials who went into the service before the outbreak of the war. Will the minister tell me?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I believe that the Order in Council only allows pay to those who were in the Government service at the outbreak of the war.

1 congratulate my hon. friend upon having learned that during the last week or two. When I addressed the question to the members of the Government previously-I think my 10 p.m. hon. friend was present,-at all events the Minister of Militia was present, and he told me he was not aware of any such distinction, and yet within a day or two afterwards I found the Order in Council passed in November-it

was published in the newspapers-stating clearly that that distinction had been made. It is impossible for any man to justify the different Orders in Council that have been passed with reference to civil servants enlisting in the service of the Empire. You cannot justify them. They had one order before the 1st of November; they have had another since the 1st November, and a different order applying to young men who have gone into the service subsequent to the breaking out of the war. These men may make equally good soldiers; there is no reason why they should not; they may do equally good service for the Empire, and yet they are treated altogether differently from those who may have gone into the service two years ago, before the war broke out. '
My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) says that the fault he has to find, or the fault which he has found, in the Northwest, is that the minister retains in the service of the department too many men who were appointed by the previous Government. Let me tell him that if conditions in the' West are at all like what they are in the East, if there had been a shadow of excuse for turning men out of office, they would have gone, and gone very quickly. My hon. friend rather admits, indeed I think he has frankly admitted, that it was because no specific charges could be made against those men in the West that they were not dismissed.
I said so frankly.
My hon. friend admits that the wielder of the axe was abroad in the Northwest just as he was in the eastern provinces?

The trouble is he has
always been abroad; he is never at home.

Wherever there was the slightest excuse for cutting off the heads of officials in the service of the Governirient, the axe was wielded, and wielded most efficiently, and many men who had been a lifetime in the service, and who had been very faithful in the discharge of their duties were turned out into the streets.

There has not been a
single case in Western Canada.

They were turned out
without any justification whatever. I have in mind one gentleman down at Ooaticook.
That is not in the Northwest.

A gentleman whose only-fault was that, in the election of 1911, when members of the Nationalist party were declaiming against the Mother country, when some of them were going upon the public platform and declaring that the people oi Quebec had only been enabled to breathe the air of liberty through shooting holes in the British flag, he wrote a letter protesting against such disloyalty; and my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, upon that ground, and that ground only, turned him out of office and sent him adrift. Such men who have been loyal to-the Crown, and faithful in the discharge of their duties, were turned out of office for no reason whatever except that their places were wanted for politcal partisans whom the Government were desirous of serving
Some of them were building sawdust wharves.
-in return for services rendered to candidates of the Nationalist and Conservative party in 1911.

(Translation). Before we put this item through I should like to make a few remarks. With a good deal of attention I listened to what the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) had to say and I find that, as is usual with him, he struck a patricularly patriotic vein in speaking of the resources in the West and chiefly of the needs in that part of the country which he represents. While finding much to criticise in the Government expenditure, he thought fit to ask at the present time grants for different railway lines that go through that section of the western country that he represents. Methinks he could have spared himself the trouble of insisting on that subject, at a time when all the country's resources go to meet the actual requirements of the war. I think it was more reasonable on his part to insist on a reduction of the expenditure for Dominion parks. And, as for me, an eastern member, I should not object to the dropping of those items which relate to the protection of forests in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Aliberta. Those residents of the West are indeed privileged. The Government pays them fabulous amounts to protect their forests while the province of Quebec does not get a cent for that purpose. Here is an item of $750,000 for the protection of forest trees in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, etc. I should gladly see that item ' dropped, when our western members;
such as the hon. member for Edmonton, are asking for a general reduction in the country's expenditure.
One hundred and sixty-four thousand dollars is also asked for 1916-17, to meet the expense of the investigations and reports on water-powers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. There is another item of $349,670 for the maintenance of Dominion parks. Those parks arc situate in the West only and are of no utility except in the West. We who reside in the East derive no profit from those parks, yet I believe that the Government could let us have a share in those Estimates. The answer was given me the other day that we pay for the western parks because they are government lands. Well, it seems to me that instead of paying for the maintenance of twelve or fifteen national parks in the West at such a fabulous price, we had better sell the land and with the price buy land from the provincial governments either in Quebec or New Brunswick. We have the same need of national parks in the' East as an attraction for tourists as have our friends of the West. We have lakes of large extent and full of fish, which would draw the American tourist as readily as in the West, if we were only given the same opportunities. I then believe that we should get from the Government a share of this encouragement, instead of all the money going west for the maintenance of national parks.
In my constituency of Rimouski are found splendid lakes, such as Metis lake and Metapedia lake, where with a little money American tourists could be attracted for fish and game, since even to-day they come there although the Government contributes nothing and they have not even good roads to get in.

(Translation). You
should vote against the Government.
(Translation). No chance.
(Translation). Why then do you vote with the Government?

(Translation). I take issue with our friends from the West who criticise a policy which is favourable to them. It seems to me that of all people they have no reason to complain. I have set out my point of vieiw, and I think it is based on common sense. We do not share in those moneys and yet those who are first to complain are our western friends.	.
The hon. member for Edmonton stated

that as the Government owned land in the West, it had to see to the development of all the natural resources in the West. I am inclined to think that it might be in the general interest to hand over the title in those lands to the western provinces instead of keeping the ownership of them and having to pay millions and millions of dollars to those (provinces. Only last year, the western farmers came here with a request to the Government for ten millions for seed grain, while in the East not a cent could be bad for helping districts which were handicapped through the failure of the crops. Those people are always applying for help to the Dominion Government on the ground that the Dominion owns those lands. I'f we have to carry such an expenditure because those lands belong to tihe Dominion, I fail to see why we should not let.them go to the provinces.
Regarding item 297, which is under consideration, I should make a last remark to the honourable the minister, for the purpose of suggesting 'that in future he favour us with geographical maps printed in French. I have noticed that for a number of years, all the maps which have been published at the country's expense and printed by order of the Minister .of the Interior are all in English. The French portion of the population pay their share of that expenditure equally with our English compatriots and yet we are not favoured with a single French map. We should be pleased, if every five or six years, there were a French edition of those maps, so that foreign immigrants from France, Belgium and other French-speaking parts could learn the names of different places in Canada and recognize those names on the map.
Immigration-salaries of agents and employees in Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries, $630,000.

How do you account
for that increase of $10,000?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The increased amount was placed in the Estimates principally for the purpose of providing for any additional boundary inspectors we might have to engage and also for any increase in salaries if they were necessary in order to secure competent men or to reward those who are on too low salaries. I am not sure that that will be drawn upon to any appreciable extent, but we would like to include it in the Estimates.
Are you keeping the same staff as last year?	'

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes,*we have a great many men who are at the front and we had to increase our staff along the boundary line, especially since the opening of the war. We were criticised here a few days ago for having a tool ax boundary inspection, and if we revise our form of examination it will entail a larger number of boundary inspectors who will have to go into the United States to meet trains there and make a special examination or investigation of people coming into Canada. In the West during the past year all the officers were engaged in connection with the seed grain work. We have our old country staff as well. A great many of the members of our old country staff are at the front. Of the immigration staff in England about 30 are at the front and we have not filled the places of any of them during their absence.
Are they in the British or Canadian army?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Nearly all in the British
army.
Do you pay them their salaries while they are in the British army?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They get the difference
between their military and civil pay.
Are you keeping the same staff in Belgium, France and the other countries of Europe?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We had practically no staff in France; we had only one agent there.
More than one.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There were four on the staff; there was only one agent.
One in France, one in Belgium?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
One in Great Britain, one in Ireland?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have a large number in Great Britain and Ireland.
Why do you not reduce the staff?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have just explained that over thirty of those have enlisted and we have not appointed any one to fill their places.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon. friend has stated that we should not vote this money unless we can get results, but he has been looking at the question of immigration purely from a European standpoint. We are carrying on a very large immigration propaganda in the United States; in fact, I have been strongly urged to double my expenditure, if necessary, in connection with the activities of our immigration agents in the United States during the ensuing year, and those representations have come to me not from my political friends, but from my political opponents. It is true that immigration from the United States has fallen off just the same as immigration from other countries, but the hon. gentleman will admit that, when a country is at war, is not a very good time to attract immigration to our shores even although the war is not being waged on our own soil, and we have been working under many handicaps in connection with our propaganda in the Urjited 'States. As all hon, members are aware, from items which have appeared in the press during recent months, owners of large tracts of land in the United States, the railway companies and the press there have been doing their utmost by misrepresentations to stem the tide of immigration that had- set ini some years ago from' the United States to Canada, especially into the West, and we have had to combat those misrepresentations by a very wide propaganda of publicity, all of which is costing a considerable amount of money. In the United States we have added to some agencies, we have opened up some new agencies during the last few years, and we have been strongly advised not to diminish but very largely to increase our expenditure in connection with immigration from that country, and, as I say, this
is not a political pressure at all in order to afford places for political friends, I had the privilege, six weeks or so ago, of attending a -conference of our immigration agents at Chicago at which the Provincial Governments were represented, and at which the whole question of immigration from the United States was discussed, and while we do not expect any large immigration from there during the war, we think it necessary to correct the erroneous impressions which have been left upon the mind-s of the people of that country, and by means of which many who no doubt intended coming to Canada have been deterred from doing so. The impression has been spread abroad throughout the United States that there is conscription in Canada; that there is war taxation, that in Western Canada there is a very large land tax imposed by reason of the war, ranging all the way to $5 an acre. All that had, to be combatted. In connection with our immigration from the United Kingdom, we cannot see our way clear to shutting up our immigration agencies and dispensing with all our staffs there. We cannot say how soon the war will end and we want our staffs ready to take up the work again immediately the war is over.
Are you practising any economy in yo-ur department at the present time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am showing my hon.
friend why it is necessary to keep on those agencies.
But you should not do so.

The minister is not
answering my question. I asked him if he would kindly tell us how the $620,000 was expended during the current year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This propaganda of which I have been speaking covers some of the expenditure during the current year.

There must be so much expended in Great Britain, so much in the other countries of Europe, so much in the United States, and so much for services along the boundary line. My hon. friend must have a detailed statement of that. I do not want very small items, but under those different heads he can tell us how that $620,000 was expended.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The salaries of the staffs in the Old Country are much the same as



t
they were before. I have the last published printed list of 1914-15 before me, and the salaries are very much the same as during the current year.

Can the minister give
us the different amounts paid?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There was paid in the
British islands $357,065; on the continent, $21,011; in the United States of America, $340,793, and in Canada, $910,009.39, or a total of $1,828,878.39. That is for the year 1914-15, and there has been very little difference during the current year.

The expenditure has
increased by nearly $300,000. It is $1,820,000 now, including salaries and contingencies.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, including contingencies.

The reason for this expenditure is that we are paying for people who are not doing immigration work at all, but who are at the front. Would it not be better for the department to state that it is paying so much for its employees who have gone to the front and so much for those who are doing immigration work? I do not object to paying the salaries of those who have gone to the front, but it is misleading to ask the money for immigration. You are paying $300,000 in Great Britain. How much of that will be applied for immigration during this year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Well, as I say, thirty of our agents in Great Britain are doing duty at the front, but they are drawing salaries as immigration agents, that is, the difference between their civil and military salaries.

I suppose their salaries would not average over $3,000 apiece, or say $100,000 for the thirty agents. In that case you have $250,000 which must 'be paid to people who might just as well be sleeping in their beds so far as effective immigration work is concerned. The people in the British islands will not listen to them. Supposing they attempted to deliver lectures on immigration to Canada, who is going to listen to them? Who is going to read their literature? The British Government will not allow men to leave the country. You are simply spending $250,000 which you might as well take down to the Ottawa river and throw it in and let it sink to the bottom.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman have us close up all our immigration offices?
Certainly I would, during the war. We have to give up thousands of things during the war.
Many businesses in Canada are giving up things.

Homes are being broken up and businesses are being disarranged in every way. Why should we keep in the public service men who are doing no good and who cannot do any good for Canada so long as this war lasts? I can understand the difficulty in the United States while the war is on. I quite agree that it is desirable to meet the incorrect stories that are being circulated in the United States with reference to the prospects of the immigrant into Canada from that country. Stories are in circulation that there is likely to be a war tax on the land-though I do not know how anybody can give an assurance that that will not take place, in view of the surprise the Finance Minister has given to the people engaged in business, not only by the taxes he imposes, but by making those taxes retroactive. I rather think that people contemplating coming into Canada and settling on our land would require very strong assurance to satisfy them on that point. Another deterrent to immigration is the fact that the" American settler in Canada is beginning to realize that his neighbour whom he left at home is placed at an advantage of something like ten cents a bushel on the wheat that he raises; and I am told that thousands of the American settlers coming into Canada to make their homes in this country have turned back in despair, and gone back to their own country. I was told that in almost every part of our prairie country through which I travelled last season. That is a difficulty that the minister cannot overcome by increasing immigration expenditure. Until these conditions are altered the minister cannot meet the objections that the Americans have in coming into Canada. When they came in such large numbers they did not dream that such a spirit of madness would settle down on the people. They are beginning to realize it, and are going back to their own country by hundreds and by thousands. If, with our magnificent country, and with the great many American settlers who are already here and who have produced splendid crops surpassing those produced anywhere in the


world, people will not come in greater numbers than 40,000, instead of 400,000 a few years ago, would it not be better for us to stop this large expenditure until the war is over and devote our money to the development of the country? In 1911, when there was this enormous immigration, the Government spent a total of a little over a million dollars for salaries and contingencies in connection with immigration, but in the coming year, with the- comparative impossibility of securing immigration, and notwithstanding the war, the declining revenue , and the necessity for increased taxes, this Government proposes to. expend half a million more- in the coming year on immigration than in 1911. Can the minister justify this? Does not he think he ought to justify it, or attempt to justify it, before Parliament? As I have said, we on this side are in despair. We ask the ministers to give us evidence of the good faith of the Finance Minister when he said that he was going to save 529,000,000 in these Estimates that would not be required. Here is the Minister of the Interior asking for millions, and when we appeal to him' for information we cannot get it. I -suppose it will be the same with every other minister. I do think the Minister of the Interior ought to reduce his Estimates by at least one-half, and if any hon. gentleman on this sid,e will support me I will m.ove

I do *move-
That the Item " Immigration-salaries of agents and employees in Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries, $630,000," he reduced by one-half.
They could enlist.

Many of them could not enlist.
132i
They cannot secure immigrants during the war.

If we were to act on the suggestion of my hon. friend and cut this appropriation in two, what would it mean? We should throw out of employment a very large number of employees who are dependent on their salaries for a livelihood. And, if the war should close within three or four months, what could we- do in the way of immigration propaganda? Everybody who speaks on this -subject says that at the close of the war we are to have an untold immigration. There may be a difference of opinion as to that. For my part, I should doubt very much that we are likely to have a very large immigration of the agricultural classes from Europe after the war is over. I may be wrong in- that. The Immigration Department deals with human lives, and you cannot deal with an expenditure of this kind in the same way -as you would with an ordinary -expenditure. Last year, our immigration -staff in Canada were not idle, but were engaged, -as I have explained, in this great distribution of seed grain to relieve the people'of the West. We pressed into service all the spare men we had in the Interior Department, including the Immigration Branch. I do not think it would be wise- to cut off the salaries or reduce them by half under present circumstances.
The men in Britain cannot do immigration work while the war i-s on.
No, but the hon. gentleman knows that all classes of civil servants who have -enlisted are being paid by the Government.
The minister is paying them full salary. These men are not making much of a sacrifice in comparison with the -soldier-s of France who are getting only five cents -a day.
Does the hon. gentleman advocate that pay for our men?
No, but when they are paid their full -salary they cannot be said to be making a very great sacrifice as compared with the men alongside of whom they are fighting and who get only five cents a day.
We are not paying those who have enlisted in Great Britain full salary. Some of our agents have given u,p their lives in the war.
But what I object to is paying immigration agents who have not work to do.
They cannot do work when they are fighting.	,

There are certain articles manufactured in Canada the importation of which Great Britain has prohibited. What would the hon. minister think of a board of directors or a manager who would insist on sending an agent to sell these goods in Great Britain? A board of directors would be financially insane if they continued to try to sell goods in Great Britain when they knew that they could not send them over because their importation into Great Britain was prohibited. That is what my hon. friend is doing in this case. He is keeping his staff engaged in endeavouring to get immigration from Great Britain when he knows that he cannot get them, and that Great Britain would not let them go even if they were convinced that it would be well for them to come to Canada. What is the use of spending money in trying to do what is impossible? If the staff can be put to some other use, well and good; but so far as the work of immigration is concerned the money spent on the continent of Europe might better be given to the war and these gentlemen allowed to do something else. I am not one of those who like to,turn men adrift, but these are times when thousands of men are being turned adrift in Canada. Young professional men are giving up a comparatively bright future, turning the key in their offices, and are receiving no salary save the small amount given to them by the Militia Department. It is asking us to be almost too humane to say that we must keep a staff in Great Britain at an expense of $300,000, when every one admits that they cannot get immigrants, and that if they did Great Britain would not allow them to come over.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The salaries to agents in Great Britain and on the continent amount to only $78,000.
But the expenses are

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That includes contingencies.
If you do away with the salaries, you do away with the contingencies as well.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This $300,000 includes advertising.
Do away with the advertising too.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It includes advertising and rents. Our expenditure on the continent of Europe is very limited.

What do the rents
amount to?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not a special note of the rentals, but I can get the information for the hon. gentleman. In France the total salaries amount to only $5,380, in Denmark $1,800, in Belgium $1,800.

The Minister of Finance appeals to the citizens of Canada to practise economy in their private 'business. This country has already been bound to large commitments on account of interest upon the large debt that is accumulating, and at least $25,000,000 a year will have to be added to this expenditure for pensions. Yet the hon. minister comes down with an estimated expenditure $500,000 greater than the expenditure of the department was five years ago, in the piping times of peace. The people of this country will expect hon; gentlemen opposite to practise what they preach. Does my hon. friend not feel, as a responsible minister of the Crown, that he should show at least some semblance of economy in the administration of his department? What sense is there in keeping offices open and paying rents and officials anywhere on the other side for immigration purposes? Great Britain will not allow any one to leave that country. Not long ago a man who was born in England, but who had lived in Canada for a long time, went home, and as a result of the operation of Lord Derby's Act, he is not permitted to return to his wife and family. Yet this Government persists in paying men on the other side, where it is absolutely impossible to get a single immigrant. As the hon. member for South Renfrew has said, there is no use in maintaining an immigration propaganda in- a country where the people are fighting for their lives. My hon. friend should reduce this expenditure and suspend these operations, which can be productive of no results until there is a change in the war situation. Is the Government ever going to economize, and if so, in what department?
The hon. minister gave as a reason why he could not economize
Did the minister appoint any immigration agents last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think that either two or three have been appointed in the United States.
Any in Canada?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have appointed a number of boundary inspectors in Canada, who are doing boundary duty at points where steamboats enter Canada or where railway lines cross the border.

Has he appointed any
immigration publicity agents in Canada?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not under that name.
In the Maritime Provinces?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext:
Who asked for his
appointment?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If my hon. friend will consult the Debates of last session he will see that I was urged to make the appointment of this gentleman; in fact when I would not commit myself to the appointment I was rather reproached.

I would like the
minister to bring down these papers. I do not hesitate to say that this gentleman's services as an immigration agent are absolutely nil. His chief occupation is that of a recruiting officer in the militia, and if he is in the employ of the Immigration Department he is doing nothing for his salary. Previous to two or three years ago suich a suggestion as the maintenance of an immigration agency at the town of Windsor in Nova Scotia never occurred to any one. Windsor has no steamboat communication with any foreign port, and no

immigrants ever enter there; yet, purely for political purposes, my hon. friend created an agency there, as he has done in other places. This agency cost $2,250. Can my hon. friend tell me whether any work was done at that agency?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: In war time the office is of no value. My hon. friend might as well throw the money into the river. This is one of the economies my hon. friend might easily effect if he was sincere in his desire for economy. So far as our province is concerned, such an expenditure in these war times is a grotesque absurdity, in view of the financial condition of the country.

The minister might well give consideration to the suggestion we have made. The position in Canada to-day is very serious. We are spending $350,000 a day for war purposes. We have a Budget of $425,000,000 this year and will have one of $500,000,000 next year. We will have a public debt, within three years, of $1,000,000,000. I read extracts the other day from speeches of the political leaders in England calling upon the people to economize in every respect, personally and publicly; yet we are asked to-night to spend this large sum on immigration from Europe, when the Governments of European countries, even France, England, Ireland and Scotland, would not permit their people to leave the country. When the war broke out Great Britain had an army of only some 100,000 men. In the effort to create an army which would enable Great Britain to make a respectable showing on land, as she could on

sea, a coalition Government was formed. That was very different from the procedure here. In England men of both parties worked together in the interest of the state. Here they seem to work only for the advantage of their own party. The Derby scheme was brought forward, -and the statesmen of England worked night and day in the effort to create an efficient army. Yet we continue in this country to pay immigration agents to bring people from the other side when they would not be permitted to leave their country. We go on with these reckless expenditures at a time when people in all parts of the country are trying to make both ends meet. I think the proposal of the Opposition should be accepted by the minister, and if the Government is sincere in its pretended desire for economy, it should drop all this immigration expenditures, which cannot be effective. The best answer to the suggestion that the war will be over in a few weeks or months is to be found in the efforts of the Canadian Government to raise the strength of our army to 500,000 men. We have 280,000 men enlisted at the present time, and if the enlistment of 500,000 men is conducted on the same lines, before we get that number enlisted, equipped, drilled, across the seas, and to the front, the war is going to last for some time, or else we are wasting our money and our time recruiting these men. I have met soldiers who told me that they had been walking the streets of Montreal and Ottawa in khaki for the last year, or year and a half, wondering why they had not been sent to the front. They said: We enlisted to go to the front, and we are still in Canada. We have thousands of men in the same position. With a Budget of $500,000,000 staring us in the face next year, the time has come for serious action, and I think the minister ought to be delighted to hold up this item, in order that he may confer with his colleagues, and see that we are asking what is not unreasonable when we urge him to discontinue all expenditure in connection with the immigration from Europe at a time when immigrants cannot be brought from Europe. During the past 15 years I have heard it said that the salvation of this country, so far as immigration is concerned, would be British born settlers, but you cannot bring to this country any British bom settlers at present. You cannot bring immigrants from the continent of Europe at present. All you can do is to bring immigrants from the United

States. Our friends opposite when in opposition used to speak lightly of the immigrants brought into Canada from the United States. They used to say that they were not to be compared with those brought from the Mother Country, that we did not know how those American immigrants would turn out in the future. We do not know what they are to-day, whether they are Germans or Austrians or of any other nationality. We do know that they are not of the stock and blood of the majority of the people of this country. We cannot get people from, the British Isles just now; therefore, is it a sane policy for us to continue to fill up Western Canada with people who will probably become good Canadian citizens in time though that remains to he seen? The best stock in this country came from France in the first instance, and from the British Isles in the second instance. If we cannot get immigrants from Britain, why waste our money as we are wasting it now. So far as salaries are concerned, Canadians are fortunate. They are being
11 p.m. paid their full salaries, and they are fighting alongside of the heroes of France who are getting 5 cents a day, and who at first got only 2 cents a day. If any sacrifice is being made, it is the Canadian people who are making it. Every man, woman and child is feeling the pinch, and the proposal to vote $500,000 or any other sum for immigration from Europe at the present time is so nonsensical that I think the Government, for its own reputation for sanity, ought to withdraw the item entirely.

My hon. friend is quite wrong when he says that we are not getting immigrants from Great Britain. The hon. member for Assiniboia said the same thing. He said that they would not allow them to leave Great Britain. Would he be sur- , prised to learn that in the ten months of the present year we have had 8,000 immigrants from Great Britain?	.

What kind of men are they?,
*

The hon. gentleman is now taking another tack. They belong to the class of immigrants that we have been getting for many years. The men are probably not of military age, but, as the same time, they are as good a class of settlers as we have been getting for many years. I would gather from the remarks of my hon.
friend that he is opposed to immigration to this country entirely.
I am not.
He condemned immigration from Great Britain and Ireland at the present time.
Not at all. I said that the men of Great Britain and Ireland are needed over there for something better than settling in Canada. They are needed to fight for the Empire.
Those who are coming here are not men of military age.
The Salvation Army are sending over widows and orphans.

With regard to the hon.
gentleman's remarks concerning immigrants from the United States, I think if he had a heart to heart talk with the hon. member for Edmonton and with other members from Western Canada he would probably be enlightened in regard to the character of those immigrants.
It is an experiment.

It is an experiment that
has been pretty well tried out. They have been coming into Western Canada for many years, and they are among the best settlers we have in the West.

They are going away
again.

It is true that many of
them have gone, but the reports concerning the exodus have been grossly exaggerated. They have not been going out by the thousands as the hon. member for Assiniboia stated. We are conducting an investigation to find out just how many have gone, and the cause of their going. I admit that a certain number have gone, and it is reported that they have gone because they were afraid of conscription. That has been assigned as one reason, but I do not think it applies to many instances. Fifty per cent at least reported by the United States immigration officials as having returned to the United States from Canada have not done so, I am sure that the investigation which we are conducting will bear me out in that.
With regard to salaries, I have already explained that 31 of our officials in Great Britain and Ireland have gone to the front, and their salaries are being paid. The total amount of salaries paid to officials in

Great Britain and Ireland is only $68,000. Of the 31 officials who went to the front, two of them have laid down their lives in defence of the Empire. Does my hon. friend want us to close all our immigration agencies, and to disband all the staffs? There are many inquiries being made at the immigration offices, and it is necessary to have a staff there to give information to those who are coming to Canada. It is true that we will not have so large an immigration while the war lasts. I do not wish to prophesy as to the close of the war, but in the event of the war being over before next session we desire to have our staffs Organized and ready for work to meet the condition of affairs that will then arise.
With regard to the vote for contingencies, we are reducing the amount of contingencies in Canada, and of the British and foreign agencies and the general immigration expenses- by $300,000. I wish once more to emphasize the fact that our immigration officials have been employed in Canada during the past year in connection with the seed grain business. That was an emergency which none of us could foresee.
You are not going to use them this year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
You cannot tell what will happen this year. I submit that it would do no harm to vote this money. It does not necessarily mean that it will all be expended. Out of this year's appropriation there will be $350,000 unexpended, and there was no harm done by Parliament voting that money last session. Nor am I going to say that all the money voted now will be expended during the coming year, but we desire to have the money in case of an emergency arising, the conclusion of the war, or anything else, so that we can utilize our immigration vote. If we were to close our offices in whole or in part, and an emergency arose like that of last year, we would have to go out into the highways and byways to get men, and pay them out of another vote entirely, or we would have to raise the money by Governor General's warrant. I dp not see the force of the hon.' gentleman's remarks with regard to immigration. As I have pointed out, our immigration has undoubtedly fallen off, but we expect that it will be restored after the waf, and we desire to be in a position to cope with the requirements and not be accused by hon. gentlemen opposite of negligence because we were not prepared.
I am not sure as to the amount of immi-

gration that we may expect after the war. We may have a considerable immigration from the British Isles, but Whether the immigrants will be of the character which we have been encouraging to come in the past is another question. From the Continent of Europe I doubt very much whether we will have a very large immigration of men of the agricultural class. To what country in Europe are we going to look for immigration? I do not know what country we are going to get immigrants from. We may get some from Russia, and that is the only country that we can get any large number from. We may get a few from the Scandinavian countries. Are we going to get any from Germany? I doubt very much if the people of Canada want them, and furthermore. Germany would not allow them to come. Are we to. look to Austria for agricultural immigrants? Austria has 'been worked pretty strenuously in the past. We did not work it, but the Canadian Pacific tried to work it and got into trouble because the Austrian laws did not permit the carrying on of such a propaganda. The Canadian Pacific were of the opinon, even before the war broke out, that they had pretty well exhausted the possibilities in the British Islands in so far as getting agriculturists were concerned, and -they were then devoting their attention to the continent of Europe, and among other countries, to Austria; But that source of supply will be cut off, and I do not think we will regret it. I doubt if we can count upon any large agricultural population coming to Canada from the continent of Europe right after the war is over We can expect a certain number of immigrants from the British Isles. I look for a large influx of immigrants from the British Isles after the war is over. It is stated that some of the young men who are now in the trenches will be so much enamoured of the outdoor life that they will not be willing to return to their usual vocations indoors. But these are not the kind of immigrants that we have been encouraging to come to Canada. 'They will not go upon the land; it is people engaged in agricultural occupations that we desire, Therefore, we want our staff retained so that we can cope with the immigrants that do come to Canada. We will have to have the co-operation of the various provinces in working out some land settlement scheme. This is one of the questions that is engaging the attention of the Commission on Economic Development and Resources.

I do not know what the report of that commission is to be, but if it recommends some land settlement policy, or something of that kind which will require a pretty large appropriation, we want to have the money available to carry out its recommendation, should we decide as a Government to adopt it. I cannot see the force of the hon. gentleman's contention that, because the war is going on just now and .there is a drop in immigration, we should wipe out the whole immigration staff, dismiss them and send them adrift notwithstanding the fact that we expect to have immigrants coming to Canada, certainly in diminished quantities, but yet in considerable numbers. In so far as the United States immigration is concerned, I am more hopeful than the hon. member for Bonaventure. He does not seem to be enamoured of immigration from that country at all; in fact, he rather condemns it.

I have heard it argued
in the House that the efforts of the Government should be directed to getting immigrants from the British Islands.

There are not less than
100,000	in Saskatchewan now.

I understood that the
policy of this Government was to have people from the British Islands brought to this country in as large numbers as possible. If you cannot get them during the war why should you continue to waste money in an effort that must result in failure? Are you going to raise 500,000 men off your own bat or are you undertaking this at the request of the British authorities or from information you have received from the other side? If you have received information from the British Governfent that 500,000 will be needed, if in a year and a half's time you have only sent 125,000 and if you have some 130,000 in this country, how long will it be before your 500,000 men are enlisted, trained and sent forward?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have to provide against every possible contingency. A soldier cannot be trained in a day, or a week, or a month, and we must get our men so trained that, should it be necessary to call upon them, they will be competent to take their places with their fellow citizens in the trenches.

Is it wise for the Government to undertake to enlist this number of men unless they have some information
that they will be required? Sir Thomas Shaughnessy says that you have thousands of young men parading the streets of our cities. If they are needed, why are they not sent over? There are regiments fully equipped and prepared for active service and still they are not sent over. If we have only 280,000 men enlisted up to the present time, how are we going to increase that number to 500,000 unless the war is going to last very much longer than is expected?

The hope of Canada in the future is in the amount of immigration that we shall receive from foreign lands and in attacking, a vote of this kind I think you are really attacking the future of Canada. All the newspapers are urging the slogan of 10,000,000 or 15,000,000 people within the next four years. In the headlines of the Montreal Star I gee that slogan every day and every paper in the Dominion is urging a similar slogan and justly so because the hope of Canada's future lies in her immigration ^ policy in the next ten or fifteen years.
What did the Minister of Trade and Commerce 6ay as to that?

I do not care what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said; I am speaking of the immigration policy which we should pursue. Are we, for the sake of the small amount of $76,000 paid in salaries going to jeopardize and dislocate the whole immigration organization at work in those distant countries which we depend upon as the hope of this country in the future? They are having meetings in Great Britain now and I have read reports pf those meetings. The object of those meetings is to get returned soldiers upon the land in Great Britain and the same thing is being done in France and other countries. The very fact that it is going to be hard to get immigration from Europe is a reason why we should keep our organization intact. I feel a good deal like my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior. I do not think we are going' to get the number of immigrants that the public believe we are. Where -are we going to get them? We are not going to get them from France because France will need every man in her reconstruction period after the war and because France will have lost so many men either disabled or killed in the war. The same applies to Great Britain and to some extent, it applies to Russia and to the other Allies. We shall have a struggle to get im-

migrants to come to this country especially for two or three years after the war and because we will have a struggle we need the machinery for the purpose of fighting our battles there. It would not be in the interests of the people of this country, of our rural population particularly to do anything that would cripple this service. I am at a loss to understand why, during the present session, hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side of the House appear to be making an attack on the rural population, When this Government brought down a Bill to tax the rich corporations, which these hon. gentlemen have been attacking in the past, we find them defending these interests. At the first opportunity we have of making them pay their just share of taxation these hon. gentlemen come to their defence. Then we found these hon. gentlemen attacking the rural mail system and now we find them attacking the farmers of this country because, if there is one thing more than another that the farmers desire, it is to have agricultural immigration coming into this country for the purpose of assisting them in carrying on their work. Yet these hon. gentlemen are prepared to cut off that service which is necessary to secure that immigration which we regard as the future hope, of this country.

My hon, friend seems to admit the fact that the advice given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day has fallen on barren ground so far as hon. gentlemen opposite are concerned. My intention, however, is not to answer the remarks made by my hon. friend. I want to get a little information from the Minister of the Interior an regard to immigration matters. A few moments ago the hon. gentleman gave us the number of, immigrants who have been brought into this country during the past tea months. How many did he say there were?
In the last ten months, a little over 8,000.

Will the 'minister be good
enough to tell me how many came in during 1914-15?

During the fiscal year of
1914-15, 43,276, that is the British immigration.
Can the minister give me the number that came into the province of New Brunswick during that year?

I doubt very much if I
have a list showing the number going into each province.

I have before me the Auditor General's Beport for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1915, and as the expenditure on immigration in the province of New Brunswick interested me, I looked it up. Although I do not know the exact number, I have some idea that only a very small number of immigrants came into that .province. On looking into the expenditure I find that we have an agency at Fredericton, one of the inland towns of the province, so that there are no vessels coming in there at all. I find that Mr. Wilmot, the agent there, is employed by the Government at a salary of $1,800 a year; that he has an assistant agent, also stationed at Fredericton, enjoying a salary of $1,000 per year; that there is a stenographer there with a salary of $600 per year, and that there is someone to build up the fires at a salary of apparently $180 for some two months. It seems to me that, unless the Minister of the Interior can give some assurance to the committee that through this agency sufficient immigrants have been brought into the province of New Brunswick to prove to the people of that province that they are getting value for the money that is being expended, the expenditure in that agency should be reduced. There are some vessels coming from the Old (Country to the port of St. John, and I learn occasionally of a few immigrants landing in that City and I know of a few who have remained in the province of New Brunswick. I am speaking entirely subject to correction and I do not want to be unfair to the minister or to the department, but I do not think we are getting enough immigrants in our province to warrant an expenditure of some $4,047 for the agency at Fredericton. At St. John, we have an agent, a medical inspector and so on, and the expenditure there is about $10,000. There is also an hospital and a detention house there at an expenditure of about $5,000, or making a total expenditure of about $19,000 in the province of New Brunswick for immigration purposes. As has been said by hon. gentlemen on this side, we are perfectly willing that a reasonable amount should be expended for immigration purposes, if results are being produced, but the objection taken by hon. members is that a sufficient number of immigrants are

not coming to this country to justify the amount that is being expended, and that therefore it is time for the Minister of the Interior, to economize, to call a halt in expenditure for the time being, and the same is true of any other minister of a department that is not getting value for the moneys expended. Every financial newspaper has commended in the highest degree the business acumen of the Canadian Pacific railway that, when hard times come to them, they commenced to economize; they laid off some of their hands, and they carried on their business in an economical manner and will continue to do so while the war is on. Every other corporation or private company throughout the country is doing the same thing. The hon. Minister of Finance told us, in the Budget debate, time and time again, that we must economize, and he said: The only way to economize is to get down to the old-fashioned way and save the cents and the dollars will take care of themselves. That advice which he gave to hon. members is good advice and advice that we would like to take, and while the Minister of Finance is not here to guide his flock along the path of economy, we would like to remind them that he has laid down the proposition that the only way in which to practice economy is to begin by paring down expenses in connection with the smaller matters to the ver^'n lowest possible amount.	, ' ' .
My hon. friend says: We have, tliese ! immigration agents and we cannot dismiss them; we cannot ask them to do without their salaries during war time. The agent at Fredericton is a personal friend of mine, and I know him very well, but, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows, he is a lawyer of good standing in the province of New Brunswick, and it seems to me it is a very poor excuse to give that they cannot ask Mr. Wilmot to retire from the office for a year or two while the hard times are on, because he can easily go back to his law practice and follow the advice of the Minister of Finance and practice economy, just as the rest of us have to do if we are not making as much money out of our professions as we did before. It is certainly not necessary to keep a professional man at the head of the immigration office at Fredericton if he is not getting immigrants and showing results for the salary that he is receiving. I am sure the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will agree with me that there cannot be enough work at the immigration office at Fredericton to justify keeping on Mr. Wilmot at a salary of
$1,800 a year, and an assistant at a salary of $1,000 a year. I refer to those matters simply because they affect my own province. If my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior cannot give me now the information in regard to the number of immigrants who have gone into the province of New Brunswick during 1914-15, he can give it to me some other time when his Estimates are before the committee.
At Halifax the expenditure on immigration is something over $20,000. If one goes through all the list of immigration offices one will find striking evidences of extravagance where the expenditure could very well be reduced. I do not think the province of New Brunswick would suffer if the expenditure on immigration was reduced. If I thought that the interest of that province or of any other province in the Dominion would suffer on that account, I would be the last one to ask the minister to cut down the expenditure. I have not had time to go into the matter at length, but it does seem to me that a very large amount of money is being expended, and if the expenditure in other provinces is similar to that in my own, I think we are getting very little return for our money.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The number of immigrants into the Maritime Provinces for ten months of the current year has been 5,198.
Does that mean landing or remaining?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Remaining. As to the
criticism of the Fredericton agency, of course that agency does the same character of work as the others. But as to the agency in St. John, that is a general agency and has to handle immigrants that are going through to other parts of the country. There is a detention hospital there which cost $4,000 or more, and that is included in the expenditure of the agency. It would not be right to leave the impression that the expense of the St. John agency is attributable merely to the work of bringing immigrants into New Brunswick.
I understand the explanation of the minister. I am obliged to him for the facts he has given me. Has he before him the number of immigrants into the Maritime Provinces in 1914-15?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The number was 11,104.
What is the number of the staff employed at the port of Quebec?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That, of course, is a very important port. During the summer

months, many vessels come there. We have a very -good hospital there, and extensive accommodation for immigrants. The whole staff there, including doctors, officials and employees, numbers about 51 persons.
Have they been decreased since last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, the staff is being decreased. I have been investigating these offices to see whether it was possible to make reductions, and the port of Quebec is now under investigation.
What is the difference in the immigration into Quebec now as compared with the years before the war?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not the figures under my hand, but I will procure them for the hon. gentleman.

I just wish to point out that while the immigrants entering at the port of Quebec have decreased, the expenses of maintaining the staff has not decreased by one per cent. Included in that staff are medical men who have their private practice and who would not be thrown on the street if their services in connection with immigration were dispensed with. I have no doubt there are other employees also in the same position.

If my hon. friend had an agency in the Old Country maintained

by a staff of ten men,, he would be the last man on earth to keep those men employed over there after the outbreak of war, if they could do no business. He would be the first one, and he would be perfectly right, in cutting the expenditure in two at least, and that is all we are asking the hon. minister to do. It will be no discredit to Canada to adopt a system of economy in respect of this service when we can get no results from it at the present time.
Follow the advice oi Lloyd George.
That is the advice oi Lloyd George and of Mr. Asquith. But hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches do not seem to take that advice.
The Imperial Gov ernment have not closed up their consular service or their commercial offices.

I am aware of that, but the members of our immigration staff are not consuls. At the present time they cannot accomplish anything, though that is not their fault. We do not suggest that when the war is over this work should not be resumed, but at a time when every man, woman and child in Canada, outside of the Government, is practising economy, why should not the Government practice it as well?

In looking over the list of officials in the Old Country, I find that Mr. Obed Smith is the highest paid official; he receives a salary of $4,000 a year. Does my hon. friend suggest that his salary should be cut off and that he should be dismissed?

I intend to support the proposal of the hon. member for St. John city to cut this vote in two, and I leave it to my hon. friend the minister to decide who shall be dismissed and who shall be kept on. I should not like to suggest that this one or that one should be dismissed, though if the minister asks me to do so, and will agree to carry out my suggestion, I will very quickly say who ought to be dismissed and who ought not. To my mind it is an utter absurdity to go on spending more money year by year on a service of this kind at a time like this. I do not agree [DOT]with the hon. member for Perth in the suggestion that it would be a disgrace to Canada if we should economize in this respect. The objection to this economy on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite is absolute evidence of the fact that while they talk of economy they have not the slightest intention of trying to practice it.
I dare say the minister is anxious to get his Estimates through.
So are we.

Hon. gentlemen are not showing very strong evidence of it. I have no doubt that the minister regards this discussion as, to a large extent, wasted time. I do not regard it as a waste of time, because if it has not done anything else it has given some gentlemen on the other side of the House an opportunity to talk economy, which they did not practise for fifteen years while their party was in power At that time they never thought of the word economy; for fifteen years it was not in their dictionary. So we should rather regard it as a good thing for the country, in a way, that hon. gentlemen opposite have had an opportunity of making use of the word economy. I think it would be extremely foolish for the Minister of the Interior to take the advice that has been offered by hon. gentlemen opposite. It would be very foolish for him to take the advice of the hon. member for St. John. In fact, I may make the general statement that it would be bad for the Minister of the Interior at any time to follow the advice of the hon. member for St. John. The last man in the world who ought to talk economy is the hon. member for St. John, the exMinister of Public Works. The man who had the record that he had when he was Minister of Public Works is the last man who ought to try to make the country believe that he is sincere in his desire for economy. And the hon. member for Assini-boia, who has backed up every sawdust wharf transaction that this country knew, and who had a very close interest in a good many deals, I believe, in the western country-the Merwin deal, the North Atlantic Trading Company, Saskatchewan iand deals, timber and that sore of thing-is a gentleman whose remarks with regard to economy we would be justified in taking with a large grain of salt. What is the use of having immigration agents while the war is on, the hon. gentleman says. The answer comes from the Minister of the Interior that in the fiscal year 1914-15 over
40,000	immigrants came from across the seas to this country, and war was in progress during eight months of that fiscal year. We find also that during the same year some 11,000 came to the Maritime Provinces, and, in the first ten months of

the year, 5,198 came to the Maritime Provinces. It appears, therefore, that even with the war in progress, we may get some immigrants from Great Britain. I venture to say that they will be a better class of immigrants than we would get from the United States. For that I have what hon. gentlemen opposite would probably consider to be the best authority in this House, that of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. Speaking in the debate on the Address this very session, the right hon. gentleman informed the House that the reason why so many Americans left the Northwest and went back to the United States was-not the reason given by the hon. member for Assiniboia-that they desired to escape the possibility of being called upon to go to war. I do not know what they are going to do now, when the United States is at war with Mexico. They will not dare to come back here for fear they will have to enlist, and they will not dare to live in their own country for fear they will have to fight Mexico. Th*ere will be no place for them, unless it be China or some country of that kind. One reason why I think it would be very unwise to cut down the immigration vote is this:
The immigration figures show that since the outbreak of the war the number of immigrants coming to this country has fallen off considerably, that in the first year of the w^r a number came to Canada, notwithstanding the war. But as the struggle became more strenuous and more severe, the number of immigrants lessened. Now, what will happen when the war closes? As has been said, no person can tell when the war will end. It may end in a few months. Does any person suppose that, the moment peace is declared, all the men who are at present in the army will at once return to their former occupations? Not at all. It will take months, even after peace is declared, to bring our own soldiers back to this country. But the thousands and hundreds of thousands of men who are in the armies of England and France at the present time, when peace is declared will be looking around for a suitable place to settle, and I think their attention will naturally be directed to Canada. It does seem to me then that, as soon as peace is declared, as soon as it becomes apparent that the more strenuous part of the war is over, that the testing time has passed, and that the services of many -soldiers can be dispensed with, it will be the part of wisdom to have our full organization of im-

migration staff on the other side of the water in order to see not only that Canada gets its share of the men who are quitting war for peaceful occupations, but that we have trained officials there to make our selection of the best men and get these men to come to the country. The matter of a few thousands of dollars, seventy-eight thousand, or one hundred thousand dollars, us a small thing compared with the interest that the agriculturists of this country have in this vote. The farmers of the Dominion of Canada to-day, especially in the older provinces, are up against a shortage of labour, and they are very deeply interested in the bringing into this country of even a few thousand immigrants. Go Where you will in the rural sections of Ontario and ask the farmer what his chief trouble is to-day, and he will tell you it is -a shortage of labour, that he cannot get the necessary assistance to cultivate the land. Hon. gentlemen opposite say, as do the members on this side, that we must have increased production. But the trouble on the farm today is that you have not the men to produce the crops. I maintain, that in the interest of the agriculture of this country, we should see to it that our staff of immigration officers is maintained, that the organization is kept up in order that at the earliest opportunity we may have all the necessary machinery to bring to this country the assistance of which the farmers of the country are so much in need.

There seems to be an
attempt to create the impression that something went wrong with the immigration to this country when war broke out. The figures I have show that there was something wrong before war broke out; that while we were increasing our expenditure from year to year the number of people we were getting on the land from year to year was decreasing. In 1911 the immigration vote was $915,000 and the homestead entries 44,479. The next year the expenditure was $1,276,000, and the homestead entries 39,151. In 1913 the expenditure was $1,520,000 and the homestead entries were 31,899. For the year ending March 31, 1915, we spent $2,103,000 on immigration and we got 24,088 homestead entries.
How many immigrants?

We got 384,000 immigrants. For the current year our Estimates for immigration are $3,150,000, and it is estimated

that we will have 20,000 homestead entries in this year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, hut he is leaving a wrong impression upon the House. He states that for the current year the Estimate for immigration is $3,150,000. Now, in that vote is included for seed grain advances, $1,275,000.

Very well. If you subtract $1,275,000 for seed grain advances, that will still leave approximately $2,000,000 for the current year as compared with less than $1,000,000 in 1911, and with 20,000 homestead entries in this year as against
44,000	in 1911, leaving the seed grain out of the question altogether. I submit that we have not been spending our money advantageously or we would have been getting more satisfactory results in the settlement of the land. The returns show that increase of immigration expenditure, if not wisely made, does not produce satisfactory results. It proves exactly what is being urged from this side of the House to-night, that the money voted for immigration has not been wisely spent, and it will not be wisely spent if it is spent in maintaining agencies where there is no possibility of securing results from them. One would imagine, from what our friends on the other side of the' House have said, that public office was a private snap, and that a man who once had the good fortune to be employed by the Government of Canada thereby had a pension for the term of his natural life. Every business enterprise, I fancy every province, certainly every municipality, has found it necessary to retrench during the past couple of years. I know that in the city from which I come they have had to cut down their current expenditures by the amount of approximately half a million per year. They have had to do that by reducing the number of employees. When times were good, a man was engaged by the city and. he had his living assured. But when times became hard and money to pay these .salaries had to come out of the pockets of the tax-payers, then, in response to the call to reduce the expenditure of the city, the expenditure was reduced. And may I say that the reduction of the expenditure by the city of Edmonton improved the credit of the city, very much to the city's advantage. (Now what is true and necessary 'in regard to a city is just as necessary in regard to this country of Canada. The Government has seen fit to add, by increased taxation, to the burdens
of the people in the past two sessions of Parliament, a sum of $50,000,000, .and they propose to add in this session of Parliament a further burden of $25,000,000. We suggest that where these enormous additional burdens are being made upon the people there shall be exercised due economy in the expenditure of the money in the Department of the Interior, in the branch of immigration, and all along the line in the Government expenditures.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) negatived:
yeas, 19; nays, 31.

The minister has made
great progress. We have put through about $4,000,000, and that is pretty good work in these hard times. I congratulate him on being surrounded by such a strong force of followers to-night. I do not think I have seen any minister have such strong support in putting through his Estimates at such a late hour as this. It is a good thing we had this vote, because a number of members took part whom we do not often see at this time of night. It is a good thing to have a variation and to see some strange faces. Some of us are here every night till this hour, and it feels lonely to see empty chairs. I congratulate my hon. friends opposite upon staying with us so late. Item 64 might go through as there seems to be no possibility of inculcating the minister with the necessity for a reduction at this time, and then we might adjourn.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Hazen, the House adjourned at 11.59 p.m.
Friday, March 24, 1916.
